entries.title: Disease burden attributable to intimate partner violence against females and sexual violence against children in 204 countries and territories, 1990-2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
entries.design: GBD modelling study (systematic analysis, spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression + burden-of-proof risk methodology)
entries.population_setting: 204 countries and territories, females aged 15+ (IPV) and males/females (sexual violence against children), 1990-2023
entries.finding: In 2023, an estimated 608 million (95% UI 518-724) females aged 15+ had ever been exposed to IPV, contributing 18.5 million (8.74-30.0) DALYs; IPV ranked as the 4th leading risk factor for DALYs among females aged 15-49. Anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder were the leading IPV-attributed health outcomes (5.43 million and 3.96 million DALYs respectively).
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly grounds the marriage-transition-as-governance-threshold rationale and the primary-prevention framing of T-PHE by quantifying IPV as a top-tier global disease burden driver; supports the rationale for P1 (decision control as a mechanism worth intervening on) but is a burden-of-disease estimate, not evidence T-PHE itself works.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms verbatim: 608 million (95% UI 518-724) females 15+ ever exposed to IPV; 18.5 million (8.74-30.0) DALYs; IPV ranked 4th (SVAC 5th) leading risk factor for DALYs among females 15-49; anxiety disorders 5.43 million and MDD 3.96 million DALYs. relevance_to_tphe correctly hedges that this is a burden estimate, not evidence T-PHE works.

entries.title: Findings from the SASA! Study: a cluster randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of a community mobilization intervention to prevent violence against women and reduce HIV risk in Kampala, Uganda.
entries.design: Pair-matched cluster randomized controlled trial (8 communities)
entries.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49, Kampala, Uganda; baseline n=1,583, follow-up n=2,532
entries.finding: SASA! was associated with significantly lower social acceptance of IPV among women (aRR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.79) and 52% lower past-year physical IPV among women (0.48, 95% CI 0.16-1.39, crossing 1), plus higher likelihood of women receiving supportive community responses to disclosed violence.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P1/P2 (governance-layer, community-level mechanisms and visibility of concerns can shift norms and responses) but the physical-IPV effect's wide confidence interval crossing 1 is a caution relevant to T-PHE's own FAILURE CRITERION discipline about not over-claiming from attitudinal/knowledge shifts alone.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms aRR 0.54 (0.38-0.79) for lower acceptance of IPV among women, and 0.48 (0.16-1.39) for past-year physical IPV among women -- record correctly reports this CI crosses 1 and does not overclaim significance.

entries.first_author: Michau L / Kyegombe N (secondary mediation analysis of SASA! CRT)
entries.title: Ecological pathways to prevention: How does the SASA! community mobilisation model work to prevent physical intimate partner violence against women?
entries.design: Secondary mediation analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial
entries.evidence_level: Mediation analysis nested in a cluster RCT
entries.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49, Kampala, Uganda (SASA! trial communities)
entries.finding: Community-level normative attitudes were the most important mediators of SASA!'s effect on physical IPV, explaining 70% of the effect on women's experience of IPV and 95% of the effect on men's perpetration; men's reduced suspicion of partner infidelity explained 22% of the effect on perpetration.
entries.relevance_annotation: Programme-theory/logic-model evidence that norms-change (not knowledge/attendance alone) is the operative mechanism for reducing IPV, directly supporting T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION logic that knowledge/attendance/satisfaction rising without deeper mechanism change (informed choice, coercion recognition) would not constitute success.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms verbatim: community-level norms explained 70% of effect on women's IPV experience and 95% of effect on men's perpetration; men's reduced suspicion of infidelity explained 22% of perpetration effect.

entries.title: Cost and cost-effectiveness analysis of a community mobilisation intervention to reduce intimate partner violence in Kampala, Uganda.
entries.design: Economic evaluation alongside a cluster randomized controlled trial
entries.evidence_level: Economic evaluation nested in a cluster RCT
entries.population_setting: SASA! intervention communities, Kampala, Uganda, provider perspective, 4 years of programming
entries.finding: Total intervention cost over 4 years was estimated at US$553,252, averaging US$5 per person reached annually; an estimated 1,201 cases of past-year physical IPV were averted (90% CI 97-2,307) at a cost of US$460 per case averted.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant background for resourcing referral and safeguard infrastructure (P5, bounded authority and referral) in a conceptual synthesis that must reckon with feasibility of implementing multi-component safeguards, though it is a cost analysis of a different (community mobilization) programme model, not premarital education.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms US$553,252 total 4-year cost, US$5/person/year, 1,201 cases averted (90% CI 97-2,307), US$460/case averted -- all figures match exactly.

entries.title: SASA! Together: An evolution of the SASA! approach to prevent violence against women.
entries.design: Programme-theory/programme-description paper (non-empirical evaluation article)
entries.population_setting: Raising Voices programme learning, Uganda-originated model adapted for broader use
entries.finding: The paper describes the rationale for revising SASA! after ten years of programme learning and research, detailing how the revised 'SASA! Together' model incorporated field learning, and reflects on debates such as how best to scale up violence-prevention programmes.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports P7 (repairability) as a real-world precedent: an evidence-informed IPV-prevention programme explicitly built a formal revision cycle from accumulated field learning rather than treating its original design as fixed.
entries.verifier_note: Non-empirical programme-description paper confirmed; abstract supports the summary and the P7 (repairability) relevance framing (explicit revision cycle after 10 years of programme learning).

entries.title: Effective prevention of intimate partner violence through couples training: a randomised controlled trial of Indashyikirwa in Rwanda.
entries.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (28 sectors)
entries.population_setting: Couples recruited from village savings and loan associations, rural Rwanda; 828 women/821 men intervention, 832 women/830 men control
entries.finding: At 24 months, women in intervention sectors were less likely to report physical/sexual IPV (aRR 0.44, 95% CI 0.34-0.59) and men less likely to report perpetration (aRR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.75), with additional gains in acceptability of wife-beating, conflict management, communication, trust and self-efficacy, and no study-related harms detected.
entries.relevance_annotation: Strong supporting precedent for a structured couples-curriculum approach analogous to T-PHE: a couples-based curriculum plus community safeguards achieved a large, statistically robust reduction in IPV; the explicit 'no study-related harms' finding is relevant evidence that couples training, when structured, need not itself increase risk, but this trial screened via VSLA membership rather than a formal STOP RULE for suspected coercive control.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms aRR 0.44 (0.34-0.59) women, aRR 0.54 (0.38-0.75) men, and 'There were no study-related harms' verbatim.

entries.title: Shifting and transforming gender-inequitable beliefs, behaviours and norms in intimate partnerships: the Indashyikirwa couples' programme in Rwanda.
entries.design: Longitudinal qualitative study
entries.population_setting: Heterosexual couples participating in the Indashyikirwa curriculum, Rwanda

Given T-PHE's own epistemic-humility/FAILURE CRITERION framing, this caveat should be added rather than presenting the finding as an unqualified positive shift.] The curriculum, designed to build relationship skills and reduce gender-inequitable beliefs/behaviours/norms underpinning IPV, was associated with reported shifts in individual beliefs, couple relationship dynamics and gender norms among participating couples over time.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] Qualitative mechanism evidence supporting P1 (a structured relationship-skills curriculum can plausibly strengthen the individual/couple-level decision-control processes T-PHE targets), complementary to the Indashyikirwa RCT (PMID 33355268).
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding says the programme 'was associated with reported shifts...over time' but omits the abstract's explicit caveat that shifts were only 'moderate, but significant,' and that 'these shifts occurred without fully transforming deeply-entrenched beliefs and norms,' which the authors say could constrain longevity of change. entries.title: Lessons learned from implementing Indashyikirwa in Rwanda - an adaptation of the SASA! approach to prevent and respond to intimate partner violence.

entries.population_setting: Indashyikirwa programme, implemented by CARE Rwanda, RWAMREC and RWN, rural Rwanda
entries.finding: Indashyikirwa combined a 5-month couples curriculum, sustained community activism by trained couples, women's safe spaces for dedicated support and referral of IPV survivors, and training of opinion leaders to support an enabling environment; adaptation was guided by the SASA! fidelity brief.
entries.relevance_annotation: Close structural precedent for T-PHE's own multi-component safeguard architecture: it pairs a couples curriculum with a dedicated confidential referral pathway (women's safe spaces) and a defined enabling/authority structure, paralleling P4 (stop rule pending assessment), P5 (bounded authority and referral) and the affected-person-visibility safeguard.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms all four programme components (5-month couples curriculum, 2-year community activism, women's safe spaces, opinion-leader training) and the SASA! fidelity brief guidance verbatim.

entries.title: Korean clergy for healthy families: online intervention for preventing intimate partner violence.
entries.design: Randomized controlled pilot trial (online modules, baseline and 3-month follow-up)
entries.population_setting: Korean American faith leaders, southeastern USA (n=55; intervention n=27, control n=28)
entries.finding: The intervention group showed significant improvement in knowledge of IPV resources and attitudes against IPV compared to control, but gains in self-efficacy and prevention/intervention behaviours, while greater than control, were not statistically significant.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to P5 (referral quality) since clergy are a plausible bounded-authority referral node, but the null result for self-efficacy/behaviour change is a cautionary complication for T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION: raising knowledge/attitudes among gatekeepers does not guarantee improved safe help-seeking or accountable referral behaviour.

entries.title: Pathways of change: qualitative evaluations of intimate partner violence prevention programmes in Ghana, Rwanda, South Africa and Tajikistan.

entries.title: Changing the norms that drive intimate partner violence: findings from a cluster randomised trial on what predisposes bystanders to intervene.

entries.title: Does marriage and relationship education work? A meta-analytic study.
entries.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
entries.design: Meta-analysis (86 reports, 117 studies, >500 effect sizes)
entries.evidence_level: Meta-analysis of RCTs/quasi-experiments (high on communication/satisfaction outcomes; silent on safety outcomes)
entries.population_setting: Mostly US/Western MRE program participants; predominantly White, middle-class samples
entries.finding: Relationship-quality effect sizes for experimental studies ranged d=.30-.36 and communication-skills effects d=.43-.45; moderate-dosage programs outperformed low-dosage; the authors flag that racial/ethnic and economic diversity was too thin to draw reliable conclusions for disadvantaged couples, and that outcomes policymakers care about (relationship stability, aggression) were rarely measured.
entries.relevance_annotation: Foundational MRE effectiveness base rate. Directly relevant to the FAILURE CRITERION: shows conventional MRE literature has historically measured satisfaction/communication, not coercion recognition or safe help-seeking -- supports T-PHE's premise that a governance/decision-control layer measures something existing MRE evidence has not captured (complicates P1/P6 by showing the evidence gap T-PHE claims to address is real).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms all numeric claims verbatim: 'The effect sizes for relationship quality for experimental studies ranged from d = .30 to .36, while the communication skills effect sizes ranged from d = .43 to .45. ... Moderate-dosage programs produced larger effect sizes than did low-dosage programs.' Diversity/policy-outcome gap directly quoted: 'a lack of racial/ethnic and economic diversity in the samples prevented reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of MRE for disadvantaged couples ... intervention outcomes important to policy makers, such as relationship stability and aggression, rarely have been addressed.' Relevance claim (evidence gap re: safety/coercion outcomes) is accurate, not overstated.

entries.title: Exploring programmatic moderators of the effectiveness of marriage and relationship education programs: a meta-analytic study.
entries.design: Meta-analysis (148 evaluation reports)
entries.population_setting: Mixed university/laboratory and religious-setting MRE programs, largely US
entries.finding: Moderate-dosage programs (9-20 contact hours) had stronger effects than low-dosage (1-8 hours); a communication-skills emphasis strengthened communication outcomes but not satisfaction; no evidence that formal institutionalization (manuals, trainer certification) improved effects, and no significant difference between religious-setting and university/laboratory delivery.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P1 (governance layer vs. content dose) and the religious-setting question directly germane to a TIMA/FIMA programme: dosage/format moderators mattered more than institutional formality or religious vs secular venue in this meta-analytic evidence -- neither strongly supports nor refutes a specific governance-layer effect, since no P1-type 'decision-control' variable was ever coded.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'moderate-dosage programs (9-20 contact hours) were associated with stronger effects compared to low-dosage programs (1-8 contact hours)... A programmatic emphasis on communication skills was associated with stronger effects on couple communication outcomes, but this difference did not reach statistical significance for the relationship quality/satisfaction outcome... no evidence that institutionalized MRE programs... were associated with stronger effects. Similarly, there was little evidence of differences in program setting (university/laboratory vs. religious).' Matches record exactly. Relevance claim correctly notes no P1-type decision-control variable was coded (honest, not overstated).

entries.title: How effective are ACF-funded couple relationship education programs? A meta-analytic study.
entries.design: Meta-analysis (32 control-group studies + 19 one-group pre-post studies)
entries.population_setting: US lower-income couples/individuals enrolled in federally funded (ACF Healthy Marriage and Relationship Education) CRE programs
entries.finding: Small but significant effects for relationship quality (d=.114), relationship skills (d=.132), mental health (d=.074) and coparenting (d=.033); effects on relationship stability, parenting and child well-being were non-significant.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports the FAILURE CRITERION logic: a large, well-funded government MRE effort shows small quality/skills gains but null effects on stability -- exactly the kind of pattern (soft-outcome movement without the harder outcome) T-PHE's failure criterion is designed to catch if applied to decision-control/coercion-recognition outcomes instead.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'a range of small but significant effects for couple relationship quality (d = .114), relationship skills (d = .132), mental health (d = .074), and coparenting (d = .033), but non-significant effects for relationship stability, parenting, and child well-being.' All d-values and null-on-stability finding match exactly. Relevance claim (small quality gains without stability gains as a template for a possible coercion-outcome failure pattern) is a reasonable analogy, clearly framed as illustrative not as direct evidence about coercion outcomes.

entries.title: A randomized clinical trial of the effectiveness of premarital intervention: moderators of divorce outcomes.
entries.design: Randomized controlled trial (couples via religious organizations randomized to PREP vs. naturally occurring premarital services; n=44/66/83)
entries.population_setting: US couples marrying through religious organizations, 8-year follow-up on divorce
entries.finding: No overall difference in divorce rates between PREP (clergy-delivered or professional-delivered) and usual premarital services; couples with higher premarital negative-communication observed pre-intervention were MORE likely to divorce if given PREP, while low-negativity couples benefited; a premarital history of physical aggression showed a similar (marginally significant) harmful-moderation pattern.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates and partially supports T-PHE. It is a key evidence source for the STOP RULE / P4 logic: standard joint-couple relationship education can worsen outcomes for couples with pre-existing negative communication or aggression -- exactly the population the STOP RULE and coercion-screening safeguard are meant to route away from ordinary joint education. Also complicates P1/failure criterion: a rigorously delivered, faith-setting RCT of premarital education found no divorce-rate benefit overall, i.e. conventional-outcome success is not guaranteed even with religious-organization delivery.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'no differences in overall divorce rates between naturally occurring services... PREP delivered by clergy... or PREP delivered by professionals'; 'couples observed to have higher levels of negative communication in a video task were more likely to divorce if they received PREP than if they received naturally occurring services'; 'A history of physical aggression... showed a similar pattern as a moderator, but the effect was only marginally significant.' All matches. This is the strongest, most literal PubMed evidence for the STOP RULE (P4) logic in the whole record set.

entries.title: Risk moderates the outcome of relationship education: a randomized controlled trial.
entries.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
entries.design: RCT (N=130 engaged/newlywed couples randomized to 1 of 3 relationship-education programs, 3-year follow-up)
entries.population_setting: US engaged and newlywed couples
entries.finding: Couples with acute baseline concerns, including higher physical aggression and alcohol use, benefited LESS from relationship-education intervention than couples without these concerns; couples with high baseline satisfaction/commitment actually declined faster in satisfaction under an intensive skill-based intervention versus a low-intensity one.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports the STOP RULE (P4) and bounded-authority safeguard: this RCT is empirical evidence that undifferentiated relationship-skills intervention is not uniformly beneficial and can be counterproductive for higher-risk couples (aggression, substance use), reinforcing the case for a screening/stop mechanism before joint work rather than one-size-fits-all joint education.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Couples with acute concerns at baseline, including higher levels of physical aggression and alcohol use, benefitted less from intervention than couples without these concerns... couples with relatively high baseline satisfaction and commitment scores declined faster in satisfaction when assigned to an intensive skill-based intervention.' Matches record. Correctly cited as direct RCT support for a stop/screen mechanism (P4).

entries.title: Does premarital education decrease or increase couples' later help-seeking?
entries.design: Cross-sectional survey study (N=2,126 married individuals)
entries.evidence_level: Cross-sectional survey, self-report; associative not causal
entries.population_setting: US married adults, general population sample
entries.finding: Contrary to the assumption that premarital education reduces later need for counseling, receiving premarital education covaried with an INCREASED likelihood of later couples counseling (a 'gateway' effect), with the association stronger among African Americans and those with lower income/education.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to P2 (private channel making concerns visible) and the safe help-seeking outcome domain in the FAILURE CRITERION: empirical evidence that premarital education can function as a gateway that increases later formal help-seeking rather than substituting for it -- supports the plausibility that a T-PHE-style programme could raise help-seeking as an intended (not a failure) outcome, and is directly usable evidence for the referral-quality proposition (P5).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Consistent with the gateway hypothesis, receiving premarital education covaried with an increased likelihood of receiving couples counseling. The association... was moderated by demographic indicators, with the association being stronger for African Americans and for individuals with lower incomes and less formal education.' Matches record. Relevance claim to P2/P5 correctly labeled 'associative not causal' in evidence_level field, appropriately hedged.

entries.title: Barriers and facilitators of relationship help-seeking among low-income couples.
entries.design: Cross-sectional self-report study (N=231 ethnically diverse newlywed couples in low-income neighborhoods)
entries.population_setting: US low-income newlywed couples
entries.finding: Top perceived barriers to seeking couple therapy were cost and uncertainty about where to go for help; direct experience with premarital education (or indirect experience via a social-network member's couple therapy) was associated with reduced barriers and greater likelihood of subsequently seeking therapy.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2/P5 (private-channel visibility, referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): identifies 'not knowing where to go' as a leading real-world barrier, which is precisely what an accountable-referral safeguard is designed to close; usable evidence base for why referral pathway design matters independent of content quality.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'men and women identify cost and uncertainty about where to go for help as their top two barriers to seeking therapy for the relationship... Direct and indirect experiences with relationship interventions was associated with increased likelihood that couples sought therapy.' Matches record. Relevance to referral-quality proposition (P5) is reasonable — the finding is specifically about pathway/accessibility barriers, not content quality, so it legitimately supports P5 rather than being stretched to a safety claim.

entries.title: The role of leaders' working alliance in premarital education.
entries.design: RCT sub-analysis (31 leaders training 118 couples/236 attendees in a PREP trial)
entries.population_setting: US couples in a randomized PREP trial, multiple facilitators
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Core numeric/qualitative claims are supported: 'couples' relationship outcomes from pre- to post-training varied on the basis of the leader'; 'Leaders' aggregated working alliance quality also explained change in relationship satisfaction.' However the record's phrase 'over and above curriculum content itself' is an inference, not a direct quote — the abstract shows alliance and PREP-training both independently explaining variability but never states alliance effects held net of controlling for content/curriculum in a formal sense. FIX: soften key_finding to 'predicted change... alongside curriculum/training condition' rather than 'over and above curriculum content itself,' since the abstract does not report a controlled comparison isolating alliance from content.] Relationship outcomes varied significantly by which leader delivered the training; facilitators' aggregated working-alliance quality (as rated by attendees) predicted change in observed communication and relationship satisfaction, over and above curriculum content itself.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] Relevant to dignity-and-consent and cultural-intelligibility safeguards and to P3: shows facilitator relational quality, not just curriculum content, drives outcomes -- supports the T-PHE premise that governance/process factors (who delivers, how) matter as much as content, and is a caution that programme fidelity depends on facilitator training/alliance, which T-PHE would need to operationalize for its own safeguards to be more than aspirational.
entries.verifier_note: Core numeric/qualitative claims are supported: 'couples' relationship outcomes from pre- to post-training varied on the basis of the leader'; 'Leaders' aggregated working alliance quality also explained change in relationship satisfaction.' However the record's phrase 'over and above curriculum content itself' is an inference, not a direct quote — the abstract shows alliance and PREP-training both independently explaining variability but never states alliance effects held net of controlling for content/curriculum in a formal sense. FIX: soften key_finding to 'predicted change... alongside curriculum/training condition' rather than 'over and above curriculum content itself,' since the abstract does not report a controlled comparison isolating alliance from content.

entries.title: Revising Premarital Relationship Interventions for the Next Generation.
entries.journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy
entries.design: Narrative review/position paper
entries.evidence_level: Narrative review / expert opinion (no primary data)
entries.population_setting: General discussion of contemporary premarital-education practice, US-centric
entries.finding: Reviews social trends (individualism/commitment ambivalence, changing marriage attitudes, premarital relationship histories, media environment) and argues current premarital interventions need updated content and structure to remain relevant to engaged couples today; offers four proposals for redesigning premarital interventions.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the conceptual-synthesis framing of T-PHE itself (P1, P7): an independent call from within the MRE field for programme redesign and modernization, i.e., precedent for treating premarital education as needing structural/governance revision rather than only content updates -- but is itself non-empirical (opinion/review), so provides conceptual not evidentiary support.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'we examine four general, interrelated social trends: individualism and commitment ambivalence, changing attitudes about marriage, premarital relationship histories, and the omnipresent media environment... we offer four general proposals.' Matches record's description as a narrative/position paper. Correctly labeled non-empirical, conceptual support only.

entries.title: Can marriage education mitigate the risks associated with premarital cohabitation?
entries.design: RCT / secondary analysis (PREP for married couples in the U.S. Army, N=662 couples)
entries.evidence_level: RCT / secondary analysis of trial data
entries.population_setting: US Army married couples
entries.finding: Precommitment cohabitation (cohabiting before a mutual commitment to marry) was associated with lower marital satisfaction/dedication and higher divorce by 2-year follow-up in the control group, but this risk was NOT apparent in the PREP intervention group -- i.e., the education program appeared to buffer a known risk factor.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates the FAILURE CRITERION in a useful way: this is exactly the kind of study T-PHE would need to be cautious about generalizing from -- it shows conventional relationship-education content CAN buffer a specific relational risk factor (cohabitation-associated distress) on conventional outcomes (satisfaction, divorce), which supports the plausibility that content-only programmes have real protective value, a nuance T-PHE's framework should not erase even while insisting content alone is insufficient for coercion/safety outcomes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'significant interactions between intervention condition and cohabitation history indicated that for the control group, but not the PREP group, precommitment cohabitation was associated with lower dedication as well as declines in marital satisfaction... those with precommitment cohabitation were more likely to divorce by the 2-year follow-up only in the control group.' Matches record precisely (buffering effect). Relevance claim is candid that this complicates rather than simply supports T-PHE — appropriate framing, not overstated.

entries.title: 10-Year Study of Christian Church Support for Domestic Violence Victims: 2005-2015.
entries.design: Repeated cross-sectional survey (convenience sample of Upper-Midwest US congregations, 2005 and 2015)
entries.population_setting: Christian clergy and congregation members, US
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Key_finding is well supported: 'Victims find strength in their faith and would rather endure the violence at all costs to keep a family or a marriage together, than to compromise their faith by leaving' and 'Clergy felt comfortable in making referrals for professional counseling.' However relevance_to_tphe overstates the referral point: the abstract's very next clause is 'while the majority of members would prefer counseling with their pastor if they were in a violent relationship' — i.e. congregants actually want direct pastoral counseling, not referral, and clergy said they want MORE training to counsel/speak about DV themselves, not that they prefer referral over direct counseling. FIX: change 'clergy themselves report needing referral pathways rather than attempting DV counseling directly' to something like 'clergy report comfort in making referrals, while members/clergy simultaneously want more direct pastoral counseling capacity — a live tension rather than clean support for a refer-not-counsel policy that T-PHE's safeguard should note, not paper over.'] Faith commitments led some domestic-violence victims to endure abuse rather than compromise their faith by leaving; over 10 years, congregational support for victims changed slowly; clergy wanted more training in counseling and speaking about domestic violence, and felt comfortable making referrals but not necessarily providing direct DV counseling themselves.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] Directly supports the STOP RULE and bounded-authority-and-referral safeguard (P4/P5): faith-based settings can inadvertently keep victims in danger when religious framing discourages leaving, and clergy themselves report needing referral pathways rather than attempting DV counseling directly -- strong real-world grounding for why joint faith-based marriage-preparation work must stop and refer, not proceed, when coercion/violence is suspected.
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding is well supported: 'Victims find strength in their faith and would rather endure the violence at all costs to keep a family or a marriage together, than to compromise their faith by leaving' and 'Clergy felt comfortable in making referrals for professional counseling.' However relevance_to_tphe overstates the referral point: the abstract's very next clause is 'while the majority of members would prefer counseling with their pastor if they were in a violent relationship' — i.e. congregants actually want direct pastoral counseling, not referral, and clergy said they want MORE training to counsel/speak about DV themselves, not that they prefer referral over direct counseling. entries.title: Culturally specific treatment for partner-abusive Latino men: a qualitative study to identify and implement program components.
entries.design: Qualitative study (demographic survey + qualitative interviews) informing program design
entries.evidence_level: Qualitative study (program-development evidence, not outcome trial)
entries.population_setting: Latino immigrant men who are intimate-partner-violence perpetrators, Southern California
entries.finding: A culturally specific, Spanish-language program integrating gender roles, immigration/discrimination context, marital sexual abuse, and spirituality was seen by participants as more relevant; the study explicitly frames cultural sensitivity as compatible with, not a substitute for, perpetrator accountability.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if it does not override consent/safety): this is evidence for the general design principle that culturally specific adaptation of violence-related intervention content is feasible and valued by participants WITHOUT diminishing accountability -- supports the T-PHE claim that cultural intelligibility and non-negotiable safety/accountability can coexist, though this study concerns perpetrator treatment, not premarital education, so applicability to T-PHE's couple-education context is indirect.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Results suggest the desirability of an empathic and culturally-sensitive approach, without diminishing responsibility.' Matches 'compatible with, not a substitute for, perpetrator accountability.' Relevance claim correctly flags this concerns perpetrator treatment, not premarital couple education — applicability to T-PHE explicitly marked indirect, appropriately hedged.

entries.title: Prevention of marital dysfunction: behavioral approaches and beyond.
entries.design: Narrative review of 13 program-evaluation studies
entries.population_setting: General review of behaviorally oriented marriage-preparation programs, mostly US
entries.finding: Behaviorally oriented, skills-based marriage-preparation programs across 13 reviewed studies showed evidence of producing behavioral changes that may help prevent marital dysfunction, though program-evaluation methodology at the time was described as only modestly improved and needing further rigor.
entries.relevance_annotation: Historical evidence base for P6 (conventional success can coexist with failure): an early review already flagged methodological weakness in outcome measurement for marriage-preparation programs, i.e., the evidentiary gap T-PHE's failure criterion targets (measuring only satisfaction/skills, not coercion-recognition/safety) has been a recognized limitation in the field for decades, not a new critique invented by T-PHE.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'The results of 13 studies suggest that behaviorally oriented, skills-based marriage preparation programs can lead to behavioral changes that may help prevent the emergence of marital dysfunction. Whereas there has been modest improvement in the methodology of the program evaluations, suggestions for continued improvements are made.' Matches record. Relevance claim (methodological weakness as a decades-old recognized limitation) is directly supported.

entries.title: Improving practice in marriage preparation.
entries.design: Narrative review
entries.evidence_level: Narrative review / practice guidance (no primary outcome data)
entries.population_setting: General review of marriage-preparation program practice, US
entries.finding: Reviews two decades of research on marriage-preparation programs and gives design recommendations covering needs assessment, timing/duration, format, content, provider characteristics, and promotion; does not report new outcome data.
entries.relevance_annotation: Background/context support for P7 (repairability) and overall programme-design literature: establishes needs assessment and provider characteristics as long-recognized levers for programme quality, consistent with T-PHE's emphasis on governance and safeguard design rather than content alone, but is descriptive/prescriptive, not an outcome evaluation.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms this is a review with 'Issues reviewed include assessing client needs, the timing and duration of programs, formats and methods, program content, provider characteristics, and promotion and marketing strategies' and no primary outcome data. Matches record and correctly labeled descriptive/prescriptive, not evaluative.

entries.title: Changes in premarital counseling as related to older cohorts of married couples.
entries.design: Retrospective cohort survey (N=256 current/former members of a Christian denomination)
entries.population_setting: Members of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), US
entries.finding: Over successive marriage cohorts, premarital counseling availability, voluntariness, and duration increased, but self-reported effectiveness of premarital counseling did not significantly change across cohorts -- possibly because marital challenges grew in complexity at a comparable rate.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the FAILURE CRITERION logic historically: increased 'dose' and formalization of faith-based premarital counseling over time did not translate into perceived improvement in effectiveness, an early empirical parallel to T-PHE's claim that conventional programme growth (attendance, hours) can occur without improvement on the outcomes that matter.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'the reported effectiveness of their premarital counseling experience was not significantly related to years since marriage. It is possible that even though the quality of premarital counseling may have improved over time, the challenges and complexity of marriage may have changed at a similar rate, resulting in no net change.' Matches record's paraphrase closely. Relevance claim (dose/formalization increase without perceived-effectiveness gain) is directly supported and not overstated.

entries.title: Premarital intervention based on attachment and differentiation improves communication and conflict management in Iranian couples.
entries.design: Quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group study (N=40, 20 couples: 10 experimental, 10 control)
entries.population_setting: Engaged couples at a university-affiliated counseling center, Iran (collectivist-society context)
entries.finding: An 8-10 session attachment/differentiation-based premarital intervention produced significant post-intervention improvements in integrating, obliging and compromising communication styles and reduced avoidance/dominating styles (MANCOVA F=8.73-42.16, p<.01-.001) versus no-treatment control.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant comparator from a Muslim-majority, collectivist-culture setting close to T-PHE's own context: demonstrates conventional communication/conflict-skills gains are achievable in a culturally analogous population, again on process outcomes (communication style) rather than decision-control, coercion-recognition, or safe help-seeking -- useful as a 'what conventional success looks like' contrast case for the FAILURE CRITERION, and note the very small sample (n=20 couples) limits generalizability.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract F-statistics: integrating F=21.90, obliging F=19.49, compromising F=8.73, dominating F=9.53 (reduced), avoidance F=42.16 (reduced) — record's summarized range 'F=8.73-42.16, p<.01-.001' correctly spans the reported values. Session count '8-10 structured ADPM-based sessions' matches. N=40 (20 couples: 10/10) matches. Relevance claim correctly flags the small sample (n=20 couples) as a generalizability limit.

entries.title: Cultural adaptation and pilot evaluation of the Couple Learning Program (CLP) among young Turkish couples: A mixed-method study.
entries.design: Pilot randomized controlled trial, mixed methods (N=8 couples primary phase + 2 couples feasibility phase)
entries.evidence_level: Pilot RCT, very small sample (feasibility-level evidence)
entries.population_setting: Young premarital couples, Turkey (culturally adapted European program)
entries.finding: A culturally adapted, 6-session Couple Learning Program produced significant improvements in conflict-resolution strategies (exit, voice, neglect dimensions) with relationship satisfaction improving only at follow-up (not immediately post-intervention); participants rated the culturally adapted program as relevant and acceptable.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture does not override consent/safety): a rare pilot RCT of a Western-origin couple program culturally adapted for a Muslim-majority country, demonstrating feasibility and acceptability of cultural adaptation -- supports P3's premise that tailoring can improve engagement, though the extremely small pilot sample (8 couples) means this is preliminary feasibility evidence, not a powered effectiveness trial, and it still measures only communication/satisfaction, not safety or decision-control outcomes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'significant improvements in conflict resolution strategies-particularly in exit, voice, and neglect dimensions-while no significant change was observed in the loyalty response... a significant increase in relationship satisfaction emerged only at the follow-up stage... involved eight couples' plus a separate two-couple feasibility phase. Matches record's N breakdown and satisfaction-only-at-follow-up detail precisely. Relevance claim correctly labels this preliminary feasibility evidence, not a powered trial.

entries.title: Perceived need of information and education about conception preparedness (CP) among engaged and soon to be married couples: a qualitative survey.

entries.title: Screening women for intimate partner violence in healthcare settings
entries.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 RCTs/quasi-RCTs (n=14,959)
entries.evidence_level: global evidence (Cochrane systematic review, moderate-to-low certainty per outcome)
entries.population_setting: Women in antenatal, women's health, emergency department and primary care settings, mostly high-income urban settings
entries.finding: Screening increased clinical identification of IPV victims (OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.79-4.87, n=10,074) but there was no evidence of effect on referrals to support services (OR 2.24, 95% CI 0.64-7.86, only 2 studies, n=1298), no evidence screening reduced women's re-exposure to violence at 3-18 months, and insufficient evidence on health outcomes or harm beyond the immediate post-screening period; authors conclude screening alone is insufficiently supported to justify universal implementation absent stronger referral/outcome evidence.
entries.relevance_annotation: Core evidentiary anchor for the T-PHE FAILURE CRITERION and P2/P5: this is the canonical finding that identification/screening without demonstrated referral and downstream-outcome effect does not establish improved safety -- directly supports T-PHE's proposition that conventional 'success' (e.g., completion, knowledge) can coexist with failure on the substantive outcomes (coercion recognition, safe help-seeking, accountable referral).
entries.verifier_note: Numbers checked strictly and confirmed exactly. Referrals: 'Only two studies (n = 1298) measured referrals to domestic violence support services...We detected no evidence of an effect on referrals (OR 2.24, 95% CI 0.64 to 7.86, low quality evidence)' -- matches key_finding's 'OR 2.24, 95% CI 0.64-7.86, only 2 studies, n=1298' exactly. entries.population_setting: health care settings, multiple countries
entries.finding: Of 43 studies across 9 categories of IPV assistance programmes (counselling/advocacy, safety planning, referral, resource provision, home visitation, case management, videos, provider cueing, system changes), programmes using a single active-assistance type combined with a counsellor/advocate reported positive results in 77.8% of studies, suggesting simpler, advocate-led interventions outperform complex bundled ones.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P5 (referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): evidence that referral/advocacy-based assistance (not joint couple treatment) is the intervention category with the most consistent positive results in healthcare-adjacent IPV response, reinforcing that T-PHE's referral safeguard, if built with a trained advocate/counsellor link, has stronger independent evidentiary support than the joint-education component itself.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 43 studies, 9 categories, single active-assistance type + counsellor/advocate combination associated with 77.8% and 83.3% of studies reporting positive results respectively. Matches record closely (record's framing that this 'outperforms complex bundled ones' is a fair paraphrase of the reported associational pattern, not a causal claim overreach).

entries.title: Intimate partner violence: counseling, community resources, and legal issues for IPV victims and perpetrators.
entries.design: clinical practice review
entries.population_setting: primary/family care settings
entries.finding: Describes RADAR (Remember to ask routinely, Ask directly in private, Document, Assess safety, Review options) as a structured clinical tool for identifying and responding to IPV, emphasizing private questioning, safety assessment (weapons, children, perpetrator risk), and advocacy-based referral requiring trained links to community resources.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports P2 (private channel) and P5 (bounded authority and referral): RADAR is a concrete, citable model for exactly the kind of confidential-assessment and referral pathway T-PHE's stop rule presupposes but does not itself specify; T-PHE could operationalize its own private-channel/referral safeguard by adapting a RADAR-like protocol rather than leaving the mechanism abstract.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms RADAR (Remember/Ask/Document/Assess/Review) tool description, private questioning, safety assessment (weapons, children, perpetrator risk), advocacy-model referral. Abstract additionally states explicitly 'Couples counseling by family physicians is contraindicated' — relevant context the record's relevance_to_tphe does not mention but does not misstate either; worth citing directly if the manuscript wants a strong contraindication quote.

entries.title: Health care interventions for intimate partner violence: what women want.
entries.design: qualitative interview study with pile-sort methodology, n=21 women
entries.population_setting: US women with past or current IPV history
entries.finding: Most women supported informational interventions and individual counseling; notably, only 9 of 17 who rated it felt couple's counseling was a good idea, with 7 explicitly reporting it was 'definitely not useful' — direct survivor preference data skeptical of couples-based response to IPV.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates the case for any joint couple work where IPV is present, and supports dignity/consent and affected-person-visibility safeguards: this is direct, survivor-voiced evidence (not proxy/clinician opinion) that a substantial share of women with IPV history do not want couples counseling as a response — directly relevant to why T-PHE's stop rule treats joint work as something to halt rather than adapt when coercion is suspected.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=21 women, pile-sort methodology, 9 of 17 rated couple's counseling a good idea with 7 'definitely not useful.' Matches record exactly, including exact counts.

entries.title: Improving Provider Readiness for Intimate Partner Violence Screening.
entries.design: pre-post quality improvement intervention study
entries.evidence_level: single pre-post quality-improvement study (no control group)
entries.population_setting: healthcare providers (nurses, physicians, social workers) at a US clinical site
entries.finding: An EMR-integrated brief IPV screening tool plus provider education plus an automated resource/referral telephone system was associated with measured improvement in provider readiness to screen (assessed via the Domestic Violence Health Care Provider Survey Scale, pre/post t-test).
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P5 (referral timeliness/accessibility) and bounded authority: shows that referral quality and screening readiness are trainable, measurable provider-level competencies, underscoring that T-PHE's practitioner-led safeguards (epistemic humility, bounded authority) require analogous structured training and system infrastructure, not intention alone.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms EMR-integrated screening tool + provider education + automated resource/referral system, DVHCPSS pre/post t-test, significant overall increase in screening readiness (p=.003). Matches record; 'no control group' caveat in record's evidence_level field is accurate (single-group pre-post design).

entries.title: Implementing Trauma-Informed Partner Violence Assessment in Family Planning Clinics.
entries.design: quasi-experimental single-group pretest-posttest + qualitative interviews (survey n=132 baseline, n=68 3-month retention; interviews n=35)
entries.evidence_level: single quasi-experimental implementation study with qualitative component
entries.population_setting: women aged 18+ at two US family planning clinics
entries.finding: A brief, trauma-informed, universal IPV/reproductive-coercion assessment and education intervention was implemented with 65% of women receiving at least one intervention element; the mixed-methods evaluation describes uptake and provider/patient experience of the assessment process.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2 (private channel visibility) and dignity/consent safeguards: demonstrates a real-world, trauma-informed implementation model for universal (not targeted) private assessment embedded in a routine service encounter, which is structurally analogous to what T-PHE's private-channel safeguard within premarital education would need to replicate, including its retention drop-off (52% at 3 months) as a caution about follow-through.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 2 family planning clinics, n=132 baseline / n=68 at 3-month (52% retention, matching record's '52% at 3 months' caution), n=35 interviews, 65% receiving at least one intervention element. Matches record.

entries.title: Patient and provider barriers, facilitators, and implementation preferences of intimate partner violence perpetration screening.
entries.design: qualitative study — patient interviews (n=10) and provider focus groups (n=29)
entries.population_setting: US Veterans Health Administration patients and providers
entries.finding: Identifies convergent and divergent patient/provider beliefs about barriers and facilitators to screening specifically for IPV perpetration (not just victimization), an area with a much thinner evidence base than victimization screening.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P1 (decision control) and P4/stop-rule symmetry: highlights that screening for use of coercive control/violence (not only victimization) is understudied and operationally harder — a gap T-PHE's assessment mechanism would need to address for both partners, not only the presumed victim, especially given the coercive-control-reciprocity findings noted elsewhere in this record set (Robertson 2011).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=10 patient interviews, n=29 provider focus groups, VHA setting, explicit framing that perpetration ('IPV use') screening has 'an extremely limited evidence-base' compared to victimization screening. Matches record.

entries.title: Factor structures for aggression and victimization among women who used aggression against male partners.
entries.design: cross-sectional psychometric comparison study, n=412 women (African American, Latina, White) who had used physical aggression against a male partner
entries.population_setting: US community sample of women who had recently used aggression against a male intimate partner
entries.finding: Compared the factor structure and psychometric performance of three widely used IPV measures (CTS2, SES, PMWI) for assessing women's own perpetration versus victimization, finding the factor structure of women's perpetration differed from that of their victimization.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates a simple unidirectional coercive-control model underlying the stop rule: shows that standard IPV instruments do not measure perpetration and victimization symmetrically even within the same person, reinforcing that any assessment tool T-PHE's stop rule relies on must be validated for the specific direction/role being assessed, not assumed generalizable.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=412 (African American, Latina, White) women who had used aggression against a male partner, comparison of CTS2/SES/PMWI factor structures, finding perpetration model 'performed poorly in assessing women's sexual aggression, coercive control, and jealous monitoring' while victimization model performed well across factors. Matches record; the asymmetry finding is accurately characterized.

entries.title: Development and validation of a reproductive autonomy scale.
entries.design: Instrument development and validation (cross-sectional survey, factor analysis)
entries.evidence_level: Validation Study (single time-point, no longitudinal outcome data)
entries.population_setting: 1,892 women at 13 family planning and 6 abortion facilities, USA
entries.finding: Generated 26 candidate items, retained 14 items across 3 subscales (freedom from coercion, communication, decision-making) via factor analysis; the freedom-from-coercion and communication subscales were inversely associated with unprotected sex in the past 3 months, supporting construct validity.
entries.relevance_annotation: Foundational instrument for T-PHE's core construct of 'decision control' (P1); the 3-subscale structure (coercion-freedom, communication, decision-making) maps closely onto T-PHE's proposed outcome domains of informed choice and coercion recognition. Supports P1/P7 by showing decision control is measurable, not just conceptual.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 26-item pool -> 14 items retained across 3 subscales (freedom from coercion; communication; decision-making); construct validity via mixed-effects model where freedom-from-coercion and communication subscales were inversely associated with unprotected sex in past 3 months. Quote: 'Construct validity was demonstrated by a mixed-effects model in which the freedom from coercion subscale and the communication subscale were inversely associated with unprotected sex in the past three months.' Relevance claim (foundational instrument for 'decision control', measurable not just conceptual) is appropriately hedged, does not claim Thai/Muslim validity.

entries.title: Psychometric properties and refinement of the Reproductive Coercion Scale.
entries.design: Secondary psychometric analysis of pooled multicenter/RCT survey data
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (psychometric refinement on pooled RCT baseline data)
entries.population_setting: 4,674 women aged 16-29 in 24 Pennsylvania and 5 California family planning clinics, USA
entries.finding: Confirmed a 2-domain structure (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation) and produced a validated 5-item short-form Reproductive Coercion Scale (RCS); recent reproductive coercion prevalence was 6.3-6.7% depending on the scale version used.
entries.relevance_annotation: Provides the field's most-used coercion-recognition instrument, directly relevant to T-PHE's coercion-recognition literacy outcome and the STOP RULE's premise that coercion must be identifiable/assessable rather than assumed absent. Supports P4/P5 (referral and stop-rule triggers need a measurable trigger construct).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 2-domain structure (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation), 5-item short-form RCS, and prevalence 6.7% (full) / 6.3% (short form) -- record's '6.3-6.7%' is accurate. Quote: 'Recent reproductive coercion was reported by 6.7% and 6.3% of the sample with the full and short-form RCS, respectively.' Relevance claim (coercion-recognition instrument for stop-rule trigger) is reasonable, no overclaim of Thai/Muslim applicability.

entries.title: Measuring social norms of intimate partner violence to exert control over wife agency, sexuality, and reproductive autonomy: an item response modelling of the IPV-ASRA scale.
entries.design: Item response modelling (Partial Credit Model) on population-based dyadic survey
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (single cross-sectional dyadic sample, non-Asian setting)
entries.population_setting: 559 married adolescent-girl-husband dyads (ages 13-18 wives), rural Niger, 2019
entries.finding: A 5-item, 2-dimensional social-norms scale (challenging husband authority; general IPV acceptability) showed reliability and validity; higher 'challenging husband authority' scores were statistically associated with husband perpetration of IPV.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly on-point setting (married adolescent couples, patriarchal marital governance) for T-PHE's claim that marriage is a governance threshold (core premise) and that norms legitimizing partner control over a wife's agency/sexuality are measurable and linked to violence risk. Supports P1 and the STOP RULE's rationale, though evidence comes from a very different (West African, non-Muslim-specific) cultural context, so cultural transfer to Thai Muslim/intercultural couples (P3) is not established.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 5-item, 2-dimensional Partial Credit Model (challenging husband authority; general IPV acceptability dimension), n=559 married adolescent-girl-husband dyads, rural Niger, 2019, and that higher 'challenging husband authority' scores were statistically associated with husband IPV perpetration. Quote: 'Higher scores on the "challenging husband authority" dimension were statistically associated with husband perpetration of intimate partner violence.' Relevance claim explicitly flags the non-Asian, non-Muslim-specific context as a limit on transfer to P3 -- appropriately hedged.

entries.title: Reproductive Coercion among Intimate Partner Violence Survivors in Nairobi.
entries.design: Mixed-methods (exploratory factor analysis, n=327; in-depth interviews, n=30)
entries.population_setting: Recent IPV survivors, informal settlements, Nairobi, Kenya
entries.finding: The US-developed Reproductive Coercion Scale transferred reasonably well to the Kenyan context, retaining a 2-factor structure (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation; alpha=0.86); 82% of IPV survivors reported some reproductive coercion.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates T-PHE's implicit assumption that Western-validated decision-control/coercion instruments can be applied unmodified: even a successful transfer required explicit psychometric re-testing and qualitative recontextualization. Relevant to P3 (cultural intelligibility) — cross-cultural transferability of coercion constructs cannot be assumed, it must be tested, a gap T-PHE has not yet addressed for Thai Muslim/intercultural couples.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 2-factor solution (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation, alpha=0.86) and 82% RC prevalence among IPV survivors. Quote: 'Psychometric analyses indicated a two-factor solution comprising pregnancy coercion and condom manipulation (alpha = 0.86). Eighty-two percent of IPV survivors reported experiencing RC.' Relevance claim correctly frames this as a caution against assuming unmodified transferability -- appropriate, not overstated.

entries.title: Reproductive coercion, gender role attitudes and fertility desire among married women in Türkiye: a descriptive and explanatory study.

entries.title: Validation of a measure to assess decision-making autonomy in family planning services in three low- and middle-income countries: The Family Planning Autonomous Decision-Making scale (FP-ADM).

entries.title: Adaptation and psychometric assessment of a sexual and reproductive empowerment scale in Arabic among refugee and non-refugee adolescent girls.
entries.design: 4-step cultural adaptation (cognitive interviews, cross-sectional administration n=339, confirmatory factor analysis)
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (adaptation study, sub-optimal fit reported honestly)
entries.population_setting: Refugee and non-refugee adolescent girls aged 11-17, Lebanon (Arabic-speaking, majority-Muslim region), including participants in an early-marriage intervention
entries.finding: A Western-developed sexual and reproductive empowerment scale was adapted to Arabic; the original 13-item, 4-domain model showed poor fit in confirmatory factor analysis, and even after iteratively removing 2 items, model fit remained sub-optimal for most domains.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture cannot override consent/safety): even careful, staged cultural/linguistic adaptation of an empowerment/autonomy instrument in an Arabic-speaking, early-marriage-affected adolescent population did not achieve strong psychometric fit, warning against assuming decision-control instruments will translate cleanly to a Thai Muslim setting without local validation work.

Quote: 'The original model for the 13-item, four-domain adapted scale demonstrated poor fit in CFA. After iteratively removing two items, scale properties were improved, albeit were not optimal. The validity and reliability results for the self-efficacy domain were acceptable.' Record's 'sub-optimal for most domains' is consistent (3 of 4 domains not optimal). Relevance claim (warns against assuming clean cultural transfer) is appropriately cautious, not overstated.

entries.title: The Reproductive Autonomy Scale: German validation and application in an Austrian student population.
entries.design: Cross-cultural validation study
entries.population_setting: Austrian student population (including men)
entries.finding: The RAS 3-factor structure was supported; decision-making and freedom-from-coercion subscales had satisfactory internal consistency, while the communication subscale showed marginally lower reliability; use in men and gender-diverse individuals was noted as constrained, requiring adaptation.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P1's general claim that decision-control constructs are cross-culturally measurable, but flags that these instruments (like most reproductive autonomy scales) were built for women and are not readily applicable to male partners — relevant since T-PHE's programme theory addresses couples, including the male partner's role in enabling or constraining the other's decision control.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 3-factor structure supported; decision-making and freedom-from-coercion subscales 'satisfactory' internal consistency; communication subscale 'marginally lower reliability'; use in men/gender-diverse individuals flagged as constrained, requiring adaptation. Quote: 'Internal consistency of the subscales for decision-making and freedom from coercion was satisfactory, while the communication subscale showed marginally lower reliability... its use in men and diverse individuals is constrained, necessitating adaptations.' Here (unlike PMID 38339841) the subscale-specific attribution IS explicit in the abstract, so this record's specificity is warranted. Relevance claim about male-partner applicability is reasonable and directly useful to T-PHE's couple-level framing.

entries.title: Evaluation of the psychometric properties of the Reproductive Autonomy Scale for use in the UK.
entries.design: Cross-sectional online survey validation (classical test theory + CFA)
entries.population_setting: 826 women of reproductive age, United Kingdom
entries.finding: The RAS was highly acceptable (>97.7% response rate) with good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.75) and fair-good test-retest reliability (ICC 0.67); construct validity was supported via confirmatory factor analysis.
entries.relevance_annotation: Further supports P1 that reproductive/decision autonomy is a measurable, transportable construct; useful comparator baseline for any future Thai/Muslim-population adaptation T-PHE might pursue, but this population is culturally distant from the Muslim/intercultural Thai setting T-PHE targets.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms response rate >97.7%, Cronbach's alpha 0.75, test-retest ICC 0.67 ('fair-good'), and CFA-confirmed three-factor structure. Quote: 'Internal consistency was good, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.75. Test-retest reliability was fair-good with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.67... The three-factor structure of the scale was confirmed on confirmatory factor analysis.' Relevance claim explicitly notes the UK population is culturally distant from the Thai Muslim target -- appropriately hedged, not overstated.

entries.title: Development and Validation of the Sexual and Reproductive Empowerment Scale for Adolescents and Young Adults.

entries.relevance_annotation: The 'choice of partners, marriage, and children' subscale operationalizes almost exactly T-PHE's marriage-transition decision-control construct (proceed/delay/refuse marriage) for a younger cohort, giving a candidate measurement approach for P1/P7, though validated only in a US adolescent/young-adult sample, not Muslim or intercultural couples.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 23 items, 7 subscales, including 'choice of partners, marriage, and children' as a named subscale, and construct validity via logistic regression association with SRH information/service access. Quote: '23 items captured by seven subscales: comfort talking with partner; choice of partners, marriage, and children; parental support; sexual safety; self-love; sense of future; and sexual pleasure. Validation using logistic regression demonstrated that the subscales were consistently associated with sexual and reproductive health information and access...' Relevance claim is strong and directly on-point (this subscale most closely mirrors T-PHE's marriage-decision construct) and is correctly caveated as US adolescent/young-adult only, not Muslim/intercultural-couple validated.

entries.title: Construction and Validation of a Women's Autonomy Measurement Scale with Reference to Utilization of Maternal Health Care Services in Nepal.

entries.title: A family planning clinic-based intervention to address reproductive coercion: a cluster randomized controlled trial.
entries.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (ARCHES)
entries.evidence_level: cluster RCT (strongest design in this set), null primary-outcome result
entries.population_setting: 4,009 females aged 16-29 across 25 family planning clinics (17 clusters), USA
entries.finding: The universal education/counseling intervention (ARCHES) did NOT significantly reduce reproductive coercion (ARR 1.50, 95% CI 0.95-2.35) or partner violence (ARR 1.07, 95% CI 0.84-1.38) at 1-year follow-up, though it improved secondary outcomes such as recognition and self-efficacy.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly instructive for T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION: a rigorously trialed, well-known couple/clinic-based education-and-counseling intervention improved intermediate awareness/self-efficacy measures without producing a statistically significant reduction in the actual coercion/violence outcome — the exact 'success on process, silent on the core outcome' pattern T-PHE's failure criterion is designed to flag. This complicates any optimistic reading of P1/P4 by showing education-plus-counseling alone is an insufficient governance mechanism in a comparable (though non-Muslim, non-Thai) context.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms non-significant primary-outcome effects: ARR 1.50 (95% CI 0.95-2.35) for reproductive coercion, ARR 1.07 (0.84-1.38) for partner violence, with significant secondary-outcome gains (knowledge of PV resources, self-efficacy). Quote: 'Intervention effects were not significant for reproductive coercion [adjusted risk ratio (ARR) 1.50 (95% confidence interval 0.95-2.35)] or partner violence [ARR 1.07 (0.84-1.38)]. Intervention participants reported improved knowledge of partner violence resources... and self-efficacy...' Minor omission (not an error): abstract also reports a moderation finding that higher baseline coercion predicted a coercion decrease at T3 among the highest-risk subgroup -- record does not mention this nuance but its core claim is accurate as stated. 'ARCHES' trial-name label is not itself in the abstract but is the well-established public name for this Miller et al. 2016 trial; not a factual problem. Relevance claim (illustrating the 'success on process, silent on core outcome' failure pattern) is accurate and well-matched to T-PHE's failure criterion.

entries.title: Adolescents' Help-Seeking Behavior and Intentions Following Adolescent Dating Violence: A Systematic Review.
entries.design: Systematic review (19 studies)
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (systematic review, but of heterogeneous primary studies)
entries.population_setting: Adolescent victims of dating violence, mixed international samples (English-language literature)
entries.finding: Adolescents overwhelmingly favored informal help sources (friends most common) over formal services; females were generally more likely than males to seek help (with inconsistencies); measurement and definitions of both violence and help-seeking varied substantially across included studies, limiting comparability.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P5 (referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): if the modal help-seeking behavior in violence-affected relationships is informal disclosure to peers rather than professional referral, T-PHE's referral pathway (private channel -> accountable referral) must actively compete with, or connect to, informal disclosure norms, not assume formal referral is the default route. Also flags a genuine measurement gap (inconsistent help-seeking definitions) directly relevant to how T-PHE would eventually need to operationalize 'safe help-seeking' as an outcome.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 19 studies reviewed; informal sources (friends) most common; females generally more likely to seek help with inconsistencies; measurement/definition variation across studies limiting comparability. Quote: 'Adolescents were more likely to go to informal sources of support, with friends being the most commonly reported source. The majority of studies found females were more likely than males to seek help; however, inconsistencies in gender differences emerged. The variation in measurement and definition of ADV and help seeking included in this review impacts on its conclusions.' Relevance claim to P5 (referral must compete with/connect to informal disclosure norms) is reasonable and well-supported.

entries.title: Development and Testing of a Community-Based Intervention to Address Intimate Partner Violence among Rohingya and Syrian Refugees: A Social Norms-Based Mental Health-Integrated Approach.
entries.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
entries.design: Co-designed, two-phase community-based intervention (workshops); RCT-labelled but abstract available describes intervention development/testing
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (intervention development/testing report; effectiveness outcome not detailed in abstract)
entries.population_setting: Rohingya (Muslim minority, displaced) in Malaysia and Syrian refugees (Muslim-majority) in Lebanon
entries.finding: A social-norms-based, mental-health-integrated community intervention was co-designed with Rohingya and Syrian refugee communities specifically to reduce IPV and encourage help-seeking, using culturally embedded workshop delivery rather than clinical/individual counseling alone.
entries.relevance_annotation: Highly relevant population match for P3 (cultural intelligibility) and P4/STOP RULE: this is one of the few studies working directly with Muslim (Rohingya, Syrian) populations on IPV-related help-seeking, using a co-designed, community/social-norms approach rather than a top-down curriculum — supports T-PHE's premise that safeguards must be culturally intelligible and community-embedded, though it evaluates a broader community intervention, not a premarital-education governance layer specifically.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms co-designed, two-phase, social-norms/mental-health-integrated community workshop intervention with Rohingya (Malaysia) and Syrian (Lebanon) communities to reduce IPV and encourage help-seeking. Quote: 'To reduce IPV and encourage help-seeking, a two-phase community-based intervention was co-designed with Rohingya in Malaysia and Syrians in Lebanon. Three day workshops, utilizing a social norms-based mental health-integrated approach, were implemented...' Abstract text available was truncated before effectiveness results, and the record's own evidence_level note ('effectiveness outcome not detailed in abstract') correctly flags this limitation rather than overclaiming an effect. Population match to P3 (Muslim minority/majority populations) is accurate and relevance framing appropriately notes it is a broader community intervention, not premarital education specifically.

entries.title: Screening for coercive control with refugee women accessing settlement services.
entries.design: Program evaluation (SAHAR study): screening tool implementation with lived-experience panel consultation, focus groups, manager interviews
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (single-site program evaluation, qualitative + descriptive screening results)
entries.population_setting: 312 refugee women accessing settlement services, Australia (culturally tailored screening)
entries.finding: A culturally tailored coercive-control screening strategy (ACTS tool, assessing controlling behaviour, fear, threats, and physical abuse) was implemented with refugee women in settlement services, informed by a lived-experience panel; the study reports screening results and qualitative service/manager feedback on culturally tailored delivery.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports the operational logic of T-PHE's STOP RULE and bounded-authority/referral safeguard: it demonstrates a real-world, culturally tailored coercive-control screening protocol for a comparable at-risk migrant/refugee population, with a lived-experience governance layer (panel input) analogous to T-PHE's participant-visibility safeguard. Useful evidence that structured coercive-control screening is operationally feasible pre-referral, though it is a screening/service-access study, not a premarital-education programme evaluation.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms SAHAR study, ACTS screening tool (controlling behaviour, fear, threats, physical abuse), n=312 refugee women, Australian settlement services, lived-experience panel consultation plus focus groups/manager interviews. Quote: 'The Safety and Health After Arrival (SAHAR) study tested a culturally tailored IPV screening and response strategy for refugee women accessing Australian settlement services... consultations with a lived experience panel and services, screening results, focus group data and manager interviews.' Relevance claim to the STOP RULE/screening-feasibility logic is reasonable and correctly scoped as screening/service-access, not a premarital-education evaluation.

entries.title: Reproductive Coercion and Relationship Abuse Among Adolescents and Young Women Seeking Care at School Health Centers.
entries.design: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of baseline survey data
entries.population_setting: 550 sexually active female high school students, USA (school health center attendees, ages 14-19)
