entries.title: Wounded Healers: Exploring Coping With Intimate Partner Violence Among Health Care Workers in Malaysia.
entries.design: Qualitative in-depth interviews (n=6)
entries.population_setting: Health care workers who were IPV survivors, tertiary hospital, Malaysia
entries.finding: Six HCW-survivors used varied coping strategies (seeking help, spirituality, avoidance, self-harm, staying/leaving); survivors relied mainly on coworkers and sought formal help only when situations became critical, hindered by misconceptions about IPV, privacy concerns and fear of workplace gossip.
entries.relevance_annotation: P2 (private channel makes concerns visible) / P5 (referral timeliness and accessibility) - supports the case that informal disclosure precedes formal help-seeking and that stigma/privacy fears are real barriers T-PHE's confidential channel and bounded-authority referral safeguard must address; also useful evidence base for the 'safe help-seeking' outcome domain in the FAILURE CRITERION.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms all elements verbatim: 6 HCW-survivors, coping strategies list, reliance on coworkers, formal help only when critical, barriers = misconceptions/privacy/workplace-gossip fear. Malaysia, PubMed-indexed. No overstatement.

entries.title: Technology Access and Attitudes Toward Intimate Partner Violence: Evidence From a National Survey in Thailand.
entries.design: Cross-sectional national survey, binary probit regression
entries.population_setting: General population, national survey, Thailand (Muslim identity modeled as a covariate)
entries.finding: Muslim identity, poverty, and residence in southern/central Thailand correlated with higher IPV tolerance for both genders; internet access (as distinct from device ownership) significantly reduced IPV tolerance, suggesting a role for information access in shifting attitudes.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P6 (coercion-recognition and informed-choice outcome domain) - complicates: documents higher IPV-tolerance attitudes correlated with Muslim identity and southern/central Thailand residence at national-survey level, which is the population-level backdrop T-PHE's coercion-recognition literacy aim addresses; supports the FAILURE CRITERION's distinction between attendance/satisfaction and actual attitude/literacy change.
entries.verifier_note: Record status is 'Publisher' (ahead-of-print, PubDate 2026-06-16), so 2026 is correct, not a typo. Abstract: 'Muslim, poverty, and residence in southern/central regions correlate with higher IPV tolerance for both genders... internet access significantly reduces it' - matches key_finding exactly. National Thailand survey, in scope.

entries.title: Maternal victimization and neglected offspring: Child marriage, IPV and depression symptoms among Salar Muslim women.
entries.design: Cross-sectional, random-effects Poisson regression (n=201)
entries.population_setting: Married Salar (Turkic-Muslim minority) women, rural China
entries.finding: Among 201 married Salar Muslim women, 65.6% reported past-year child neglect, 30.8% reported past-year IPV, and 37.6% had experienced child marriage; child marriage and IPV victimization were associated with downstream child-neglect risk.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P4 (decision control and STOP RULE) - supports: shows a documented pathway in a Muslim minority population from child marriage through IPV to intergenerational harm, reinforcing why T-PHE frames marriage entry as a governance threshold requiring decision control and a coercion/violence stop rule rather than treating marriage completion as automatically protective.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'reported a 65.6% rate of child neglect and a 30.8% rate of IPV in the past year. 37.6% experienced child marriage... significant associations between child neglect and child marriage, IPV, and depression symptoms.' All three percentages and the association claim match exactly. Correctly identified as rural China (Salar Muslim minority), not Southeast Asia -- relevance framing does not overstate region.

entries.title: Child Marriage in South Asia: A Systematic Review.
entries.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
entries.design: Systematic review (PRISMA, 13 included studies of 520 screened), PROSPERO CRD42020190410
entries.population_setting: South Asian populations (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka), including Muslim subgroups
entries.finding: Consistent correlates of child marriage were rural residence, low education, poor economic background, low mass-media exposure and religion (Hindu and Muslim in particular countries); downstream maternal-health effects included lower antenatal care use, institutional delivery and skilled birth attendance.
entries.relevance_annotation: P7 (repairability) / FAILURE CRITERION - supports the broader evidence base that child/early marriage clusters with reduced maternal-health-service use, relevant to why T-PHE frames reproductive-health literacy (not just knowledge/attendance) as a required outcome domain; regional (South Asia, not Southeast Asia) so context-adjacent rather than direct.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Factors consistently associated with child marriage in South Asia were rural residence, low level of education, poor economic background, low exposure to mass media and religion... low utilization of antenatal care services, low institutional delivery, and low delivery assistance by a skilled birth attendant.' Matches key_finding closely. Record's own relevance text honestly flags 'regional (South Asia, not Southeast Asia) so context-adjacent rather than direct' -- no overstatement of geographic fit.

entries.title: Factors influencing sexual and reproductive health of Muslim women: a systematic review.
entries.design: Systematic review, narrative synthesis (59 studies, 22 countries)
entries.population_setting: Muslim women, multi-country (worldwide, including Southeast/South Asian settings)
entries.finding: Across 59 studies from 22 countries, many Muslim women had poor sexual and reproductive health (SRH) knowledge and negative attitudes shaping service access; religious and cultural beliefs, family and community were recurring barriers to contraception use and SRH service/information access.
entries.relevance_annotation: P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture cannot override consent/safety) / FAILURE CRITERION reproductive-health-literacy domain - supports: documents the global evidence base that cultural/religious framing shapes SRH knowledge gaps in Muslim populations, which is the literacy gap T-PHE's failure criterion targets as a required outcome distinct from attendance/satisfaction.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: '59 studies were included from 22 countries... Many Muslim women have poor SRH knowledge, and negative attitudes... Religious and cultural beliefs were barriers to contraception use and access to SRH services and information.' Matches key_finding. Global systematic review, in scope, relevance framing appropriately generic (not claimed Thailand-specific).

entries.title: A qualitative study on perceptions of adolescents' sexual and reproductive health education in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
entries.journal: International Journal of Adolescent Medicine and Health
entries.design: Qualitative (focus groups and individual interviews, feminist analytic lens), fieldwork 2016
entries.population_setting: Javanese Muslim adolescents and adults, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
entries.finding: School-based SRH education in the Javanese Muslim community was constrained by taboo and moral-panic framing around premarital sex; delivery gaps left adolescents without reliable sexuality information despite peer-counsellor programmes intended to fill this role.
entries.relevance_annotation: P3 (cultural intelligibility vs consent/safety boundary) - complicates: shows that in a comparable Southeast Asian Muslim-majority setting, culturally cautious SRH-education framing can itself suppress the informed-choice/reproductive-literacy content T-PHE's failure criterion requires, illustrating the tension P3 explicitly flags (cultural tailoring must not override the substance of informed choice).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'contentious due to societal and religious taboos... misunderstood as a potential catalyst for premarital sex... Peer counsellors... reproduced adult moral values toward their peers, leading to a reluctance among adolescents to share their issues. Consequently, SRH education failed to reach those experiencing unwanted pregnancy or a toxic intimate relationship.' Matches key_finding's taboo/moral-panic and peer-counsellor-gap framing precisely.

entries.title: Intimate Partner Violence among Canadian Muslim Women.
entries.design: Qualitative dominant design with supplemental quantitative data (n=8)
entries.evidence_level: Qualitative study with descriptive quantitative supplement
entries.population_setting: Canadian Muslim immigrant women, 6 countries of origin
entries.finding: Pre-migration adverse childhood experiences and family history of IPV, combined with post-migration language/social-isolation barriers and internalized patriarchal values, shaped help-seeking and the eventual decision to leave abusive relationships among 8 Muslim immigrant women.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P5 (decision control and referral quality: timeliness, accessibility, follow-through) - supports: documents concrete pre- and post-marriage barriers to disclosure and help-seeking in Muslim women, reinforcing why T-PHE frames accountable referral (not just availability) as a distinct success criterion from attendance/satisfaction.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms pre-migration ACEs/family IPV history, post-migration language/isolation barriers and internalized patriarchal values shaping help-seeking and the decision to leave. Population correctly stated as Canadian immigrant Muslim women (not Southeast Asia); relevance text does not claim regional fit, only thematic (help-seeking/decision-control) relevance.

entries.title: Muslim Women's Experiences of Domestic Violence and Abuse: A Meta-Ethnography of Global Evidence.
entries.design: Meta-ethnography (33 qualitative studies synthesized), 6 databases searched
entries.population_setting: Muslim women, global (multi-country qualitative evidence)
entries.finding: Synthesis of 33 qualitative studies identified four major themes - experience/impact of abuse, risk factors, help-seeking, and coping - and found religion functions both as a risk factor for abuse and a barrier to help-seeking, and simultaneously as a coping resource for some women.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P3/P5 (decision control, cultural intelligibility vs safety, referral quality) - supports: the dual role of religion (barrier and resource) directly substantiates T-PHE's epistemic-humility and cultural-intelligibility safeguards, and the help-seeking/coping themes ground the FAILURE CRITERION's coercion-recognition and safe-help-seeking outcome domains in Muslim populations specifically.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: '33 qualitative studies... four major themes: the experience and impacts of abuse; risk factors...; help-seeking; and the coping strategies... religion not only as a risk factor for violence and a barrier to help-seeking but also as a coping strategy.' Matches key_finding's 'four major themes' and dual-role-of-religion claim exactly.

entries.title: Shame, Family Honor, and Dating Abuse: Lessons From an Exploratory Study of South Asian Muslims.
entries.design: Exploratory qualitative study
entries.population_setting: South Asian Muslim communities (diaspora)
entries.finding: Cultural norms constructing dating as shameful were found to intensify fear of parental/community reaction and strengthen attachment to abusive partners, with direct implications for disclosure, help-seeking, and the ability to end abusive relationships.
entries.relevance_annotation: P4 (STOP RULE) / P1 (decision control) - supports: illustrates the mechanism by which family-honor and shame norms can suppress disclosure of coercion/abuse before or during a relationship transition, which is precisely the risk the STOP RULE (pause joint work pending confidential assessment) is designed to interrupt.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'cultural norms may prompt fear of parental and community reactions to dating as well as strong relationship attachment. These then have implications for disclosure, help seeking, and ending abusive relationships.' Matches key_finding. Correctly labeled as South Asian Muslim diaspora, not Thailand/Southeast Asia.

entries.title: Establishing a one-stop crisis center for women suffering violence in Khonkaen hospital, Thailand.
entries.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
entries.design: Intervention/comparison case-site description
entries.population_setting: Women experiencing physical or sexual assault, Khon Kaen provincial hospital, Thailand
entries.finding: Describes the establishment and early operation of a hospital-based One Stop Crisis Center (OSCC) for women survivors of violence in Khon Kaen, Thailand, compared against a non-intervention provincial hospital site.
entries.relevance_annotation: P5 (referral quality: timeliness, accessibility, follow-through) - supports: this is the founding Thai literature on the OSCC model referenced by the angle brief; directly relevant to what an accountable, bounded-authority referral pathway looks like operationally in Thailand, which T-PHE's safeguards must interface with rather than replace.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'discusses the experiences of the Khonkaen provincial hospital, which has been selected as an intervention case site for a one-stop crisis service... compared with another provincial hospital where no intervention has taken place.' Matches key_finding directly. Thailand, PubMed-indexed, on-topic OSCC evidence.

entries.title: [Domestic violence as a women's health issue--activities of health professionals in Thailand].
entries.journal: Japanese Journal of Public Health (Nihon Koshu Eisei Zasshi)
entries.design: Qualitative interview study
entries.population_setting: Abused women and health/legal/community actors, Khon Kaen province, northeastern Thailand
entries.finding: Interviews with 4 abused women and surrounding health professionals, government/legal staff and community members in Khon Kaen showed health professionals (nurses, community health workers) and, in one case, a community religious leader (a Buddhist monk) played identifiable roles in identifying, treating and supporting abused women within a multi-actor referral network.
entries.relevance_annotation: P5 (referral quality) / safeguard: bounded authority and referral - supports: provides a concrete Thai example of a multi-actor DV-response network (health worker + community/religious figure), a template relevant to how T-PHE's referral safeguard should interface with existing Thai local response networks rather than creating a parallel pathway.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'We interviewed 4 abused women... Another woman was successfully supported by nurses of the health center, a community leader and a Buddhist monk. Health professionals played important roles in identifying, treating and protecting abused women.' The key_finding's 'in one case, a community religious leader (a Buddhist monk)' correctly hedges to a single case, not a general claim -- accurate, not overstated.

entries.title: "Hitting as Light as Feathers": Religious Leaders' Voices on Domestic Violence.
entries.design: Qualitative in-depth interviews (n=13 male religious leaders)
entries.population_setting: Male religious leaders across multiple faith denominations, Lebanon
entries.finding: Thirteen religious leaders reported routinely counseling on marital/familial problems and described mixed responses to DV (from minimizing rhetoric captured in the title quote to referral to legal measures), highlighting variable readiness among faith leaders to recognize and respond to DV.
entries.relevance_annotation: Safeguard: bounded authority and referral / epistemic humility - complicates: not Southeast Asia, but directly evidences the risk T-PHE's bounded-authority safeguard is designed against - faith leaders acting as de facto first responders to DV without consistent recognition or referral practice, underscoring why joint marital counseling must not substitute for a competent safety assessment.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: '13 male religious leaders... All of the participants stated that they were involved in the affairs of their communities by counseling on familial and marital problems... responding to DV through counseling and taking legal measures.' Matches key_finding. Lebanon, correctly flagged in the record as 'not Southeast Asia... complicates' rather than presented as direct regional evidence. No named individual or organisation criticized; discussion is of religious leaders as an occupational group in aggregate.

entries.title: An empirical exploration of female child marriage determinants in Indonesia.
entries.design: Cross-sectional secondary analysis, multivariate regression (nationally representative, n=6,578)
entries.population_setting: Women aged 20-24, Indonesia (2012 Indonesian Demographic and Health Survey / Adolescent Reproductive Health Survey)
entries.finding: In a nationally representative Indonesian sample, approximately 17% of women were married before age 18 and 6% before age 16; the paper notes research on child marriage in Southeast Asia specifically was scarce prior to this nationally representative multivariate analysis.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P4 (marriage transition as governance threshold; STOP RULE) - supports: nationally representative Southeast Asian (Indonesia) baseline data on the prevalence of marriage before the age of full decision-capacity, directly grounding T-PHE's claim that the marriage transition is a genuine governance threshold in the region the abstract targets.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'approximately 17% and 6% report being married before 18 and 16 years old respectively... Research on child marriage in Southeast Asia is scarce.' Matches key_finding's prevalence figures and the 'scarce prior research' framing exactly. Nationally representative Indonesia data, in scope.

entries.title: Marriage is not a safe place: heterosexual marriage and HIV-related vulnerability in Indonesia.
entries.design: Documentary/archival analysis and expert-informant interviews
entries.population_setting: Married women, Indonesia (Muslim-majority context)
entries.finding: Traditional practices including polygamy, early marriage and contract marriage (mut'a) were identified as enhancing married Indonesian women's likelihood of HIV acquisition within marriage, challenging the assumption that marital status is protective.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P6 (conventional success can coexist with failure) - supports: directly substantiates T-PHE's proposition that marriage completion is not itself evidence of a good outcome; reproductive/health-literacy and safety risks can persist or increase after marriage in a Southeast Asian Muslim-majority setting, reinforcing the FAILURE CRITERION's separation of completion from literacy/safety outcomes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'traditional practices such as polygamy, early marriage and contract marriage (mut'a) play an important role in enhancing women's likelihood of acquiring HIV within the Indonesian context.' Matches key_finding. Indonesia, in scope; relevance claim (marriage completion not evidence of good outcome) is a reasonable reading, not overstated.

entries.title: Cultural and religious determinants of HIV transmission: A qualitative study with people living with HIV in Belu and Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
entries.design: Qualitative in-depth interviews (n=92: 52 women, 40 men)
entries.population_setting: People living with HIV, Belu and Yogyakarta, Indonesia (Islamic and Javanese cultural context)

Islamic religious beliefs about expected husband-wife relationships, forbidden premarital sex, and... condom use... contributed to HIV transmission.' Matches key_finding. Indonesia, in scope.

entries.title: Regulation of sexuality in Indonesian discourse: normative gender, criminal law and shifting strategies of control.

entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms the historical-discourse trajectory: New Order gender/heterosexuality-marriage linkage -> 1990s Islamic-discourse shifts -> post-1998 push for criminal-code restrictions on sexuality. Matches key_finding. Record's own relevance text correctly labels this 'not empirical outcome data,' avoiding overclaim.

entries.title: Prevalence of and factors associated with female child marriage in Indonesia.

entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'prevalence of female child marriage in Indonesia was quite high, reaching about 12.53%... health insurance and sex of household head did not significantly influence female child marriage.' entries.title: Factors affecting child marriage and contraceptive use among Rohingya girls in refugee camps.

entries.relevance_annotation: supports Layer 0 self-check design (self-directed reflection + individualised readout the person controls) and the private-channel/R2 concept; also the direct methodological ancestor of the T-PHE self-check model.
entries.verifier_note: Protocol paper. Abstract: 'Primary self-reported outcomes are: self-efficacy ... immediately after completion, 6 and 12 months post-baseline; and depressive symptoms ... 6 and 12 months post-baseline.' Design/self-directed description matches. No outcome claims made, so record correctly stays at protocol-level evidence.

entries.title: An online healthy relationship tool and safety decision aid for women experiencing intimate partner violence (I-DECIDE): a randomised controlled trial.
entries.design: Pragmatic 2-arm RCT (masked, ITT), n=422 randomised (227 intervention/195 control)
entries.population_setting: Women 16-50y screening positive for IPV or partner fear in Australia, entirely web-based recruitment/delivery
entries.finding: 79-80% 12-month retention; self-efficacy was NOT improved and was in fact slightly LOWER in the intervention group than control at 6 months (mean difference 1.3, 95%CI 0.3-2.3) and 12 months (1.6, 95%CI 0.5-2.7); no between-group difference in depressive symptoms at 6 or 12 months.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates the assumption that an online self-assessment/decision aid improves self-efficacy or mental-health outcomes on validated quantitative measures - a null/adverse-direction primary-outcome result from the flagship trial in this literature; supports feasibility of anonymous web-only recruitment and high retention as a delivery model for Layer 0/R2.
entries.verifier_note: Numbers verified verbatim. Abstract: 'Mean self-efficacy at 6 months and 12 months was lower for participants in the intervention group than for participants in the control group ... (6 months: 27·5 [SD 5·1] vs 28·1 [4·4], imputed mean difference 1·3 [95% CI 0·3 to 2·3]; 12 months: 27·8 [SD 5·4] vs 29·0 [5·0], imputed mean difference 1·6 [95% CI 0·5 to 2·7])' and '179 (79%) ... in the intervention group and 156 (80%) ... in the control group completed 12-month follow-up' and 'no difference between groups in depressive symptoms at 6 months or 12 months'. Direction (lower self-efficacy in intervention arm, i.e. adverse-direction/null) correctly stated. Relevance claim correctly frames this as complicating (not disproving) the assumption, and does not overstate Australia-trial results as generalizable to a Thai premarital self-check.

entries.title: I-DECIDE: An Online Intervention Drawing on the Psychosocial Readiness Model for Women Experiencing Domestic Violence.
entries.design: Theoretical/conceptual development article
entries.population_setting: Conceptual - women experiencing domestic violence, informs the I-DECIDE Australian trial
entries.finding: Argues that internet delivery can overcome disclosure barriers present in face-to-face health-care settings by letting a woman assess readiness and situate a plan within the Psychosocial Readiness Model before any external contact.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports the theoretical rationale for Layer 0 (self-check precedes and may substitute for disclosure to any programme actor) and for the person, not the programme, holding the readout.
entries.verifier_note: Theoretical/conceptual paper, correctly labeled non-empirical. Abstract: 'the Internet as a method of intervention delivery for DV might overcome many of the barriers present in health care settings. Using the PRM as a framework for an online DV intervention may help women on a pathway to safety and well-being for themselves and their children.' Key finding is a fair paraphrase; relevance claim is appropriately framed as theoretical rationale, not an efficacy claim.

entries.title: A safety app to respond to dating violence for college women and their friends: the MyPlan study randomized controlled trial protocol.
entries.design: RCT protocol
entries.population_setting: 300 abused college women + 300 concerned friends, Maryland and Oregon, USA
entries.finding: Describes myPlan, a self-administered web/smartphone safety decision aid where users enter relationship-health and safety information and receive a personalised, priority-weighted safety plan they control, versus a static safety-planning control site.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports the scored, self-held-readout design pattern (user enters data, sees own tailored output) that Layer 0 adapts to premarital fear/control/reproductive/mental-health domains.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Three hundred female college students experiencing abuse and three hundred friends ... will be recruited in Maryland and Oregon' matches population_setting. App description (relationship health, safety priorities, severity of violence inputs -> personalized safety plan) matches key_finding. Protocol paper, no outcome overclaim.

entries.title: Longitudinal Impact of the myPlan App on Health and Safety Among College Women Experiencing Partner Violence.
entries.design: RCT, longitudinal follow-up

entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Reproductive-coercion reduction is correctly reported as significant. The abstract also reports a greater improvement in suicide risk in the myPlan group, but its own stated p-value (p=.46) does not support significance for that outcome - flagged here as an internal inconsistency in the source abstract, not a verified significant suicide-risk effect.

entries.title: Concerned friends of intimate partner violence survivors: results from the myPlan randomized controlled trial on college campuses.
entries.design: RCT, sub-study on friends/bystanders
entries.population_setting: 293 college students (any gender) who were friends of an IPV survivor, 41 Oregon/Maryland colleges
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: 89.2%/22.7% figures verified exactly. Correction: change key_finding's 'myPlan-assigned friends showed significantly greater improvement in decisional conflict/understanding' to 'showed greater improvement in decisional conflict/understanding and decisional preparedness (not stated as statistically significant in the abstract), and a significantly greater increase in confidence to talk about their own relationship concerns at 12 months.'] 89.2% of concerned friends worried their friend would be seriously hurt (22.7% extreme concern); myPlan-assigned friends showed greater improvement in decisional conflict/understanding and decisional preparedness (not stated as statistically significant in the abstract), and a significantly greater increase in confidence to talk with someone about their own relationship concerns at 12 months.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] complicates a person-only framing - shows a decision-aid model also functions for third parties (peers/family) who might carry a Layer 0 readout forward, relevant to how a T-PHE self-check result could be shared voluntarily with a trusted other.
entries.verifier_note: 89.2%/22.7% figures verified exactly. entries.title: Effectiveness of the myPlan Teen App, a Digital Healthy Relationship and Safety Planning Intervention With Adolescent Aged 15-17 Years.
entries.design: Longitudinal RCT
entries.population_setting: 617 adolescents aged 15-17y, myPlan Teen vs usual care, USA
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Minor title mismatch: search file has 'Adolescents Aged 15-17 Years' (plural); PubMed ArticleTitle is 'Adolescent Aged 15-17 Years' (singular, likely a typo in the published title itself). entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] supports feasibility and selected efficacy of a self-directed digital safety/relationship tool in an adolescent (pre-adult, premarital-adjacent) population, though on a mixed outcome pattern - some outcomes null, informing T-PHE's own honest failure criterion.

entries.title: Adapting the myPlan safety app to respond to intimate partner violence for women in low and middle income country settings: app tailoring and randomized controlled trial protocol.
entries.design: Formative adaptation study + RCT protocol
entries.population_setting: Women reporting IPV/fear of partner, urban informal settlement, Nairobi, Kenya (LMIC)
entries.finding: Community-participatory adaptation found high feasibility and acceptability of a technology-based self-assessment/safety-planning tool in a low-literacy LMIC setting, requiring simplified content, increased visualisation, and delivery via community health volunteers rather than pure self-use.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports transferability of self-check/decision-aid tools to LMIC and non-Western contexts relevant to Thailand, but complicates a pure self-administered (person-alone) Layer 0 model - LMIC adaptation required facilitated/CHV-supported delivery for feasibility.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms: 'Formative phase revealed high feasibility and acceptability of a technology-based intervention for safety planning in this LMIC setting. This phase generated essential refinements ... including increased visualization of messaging, and implementation via community health volunteers (CHVs).' Relevance claim correctly flags that this required facilitated/CHV-supported delivery, appropriately complicating (not overclaiming) transfer to a pure self-administered Layer 0 model.

entries.title: Safety decision-making and planning mobile app for intimate partner violence prevention and response: randomised controlled trial in Kenya.
entries.design: Randomised, participant-blinded superiority trial, n=352 (177 intervention/175 control), 88.6% retained at 3 months
entries.population_setting: Women at risk of/experiencing IPV, Nairobi, Kenya (LMIC, low-resource urban)
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: All numbers verified exactly (n=352, 177/175, 88.6% retention, p=0.001, p=0.004, p<0.01 x2). However the abstract states this intervention was 'administrated by trained lay professionals' (facilitated, not self-administered) - this fact is omitted from both the design field and the relevance_to_tphe claim. Relevance overstates transfer: T-PHE Layer 0 is an anonymous, unfacilitated self-check, while myPlan Kenya's positive safety/lethality results come from a facilitator-led delivery model. Correction: add to design/key_finding that delivery was facilitator-administered, and revise relevance_to_tphe to note this weakens (does not eliminate) direct relevance to an anonymous, self-only Layer 0 design - it evidences the facilitated variant of this tool class, not the self-directed one.] Intervention was administered by trained lay professionals (facilitator-delivered, not self-administered). The facilitator-delivered group had significantly better immediate post-intervention safety preparedness (p=0.001) and 3-month helpfulness of safety strategies (p=0.004); among women with the highest baseline IPV severity, the facilitator-delivered intervention significantly increased resilience (p<0.01) and significantly decreased risk for lethal violence (p<0.01).
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] provides evidence for the facilitator-delivered variant of this tool class, not a self-directed one: myPlan Kenya's safety/lethality results come from lay-professional-administered delivery, which weakens (does not eliminate) direct relevance to T-PHE's anonymous, unfacilitated Layer 0 self-check design.
entries.verifier_note: All numbers verified exactly (n=352, 177/175, 88.6% retention, p=0.001, p=0.004, p<0.01 x2). However the abstract states this intervention was 'administrated by trained lay professionals' (facilitated, not self-administered) - this fact is omitted from both the design field and the relevance_to_tphe claim. entries.title: A tailored online safety and health intervention for women experiencing intimate partner violence: the iCAN Plan 4 Safety randomized controlled trial protocol.
entries.design: Double-blind RCT protocol, n=450 planned
entries.population_setting: Canadian women who experienced IPV in previous 6 months, including rural/Indigenous/racialized/immigrant/privacy-prioritising subgroups
entries.finding: Notes fewer than 1 in 5 Canadian women access safety planning through formal DV services, motivating a tailored, interactive, self-paced online intervention (iCAN) that lets women build risk awareness and a personalised action plan without needing to contact services first.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports the rationale for an anonymous, low-barrier self-check that reaches people who would not otherwise contact a formal service - directly parallel to Layer 0's function as an entry point independent of programme staff.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract verbatim: 'fewer than 1 in 5 Canadian women access safety planning through domestic violence services.' n=450 matches. Protocol paper, no outcome overclaim.

entries.title: Longitudinal impacts of an online safety and health intervention for women experiencing intimate partner violence: randomized controlled trial.
entries.design: Double-blind RCT, n=462 Canadian women
entries.population_setting: Adult Canadian women with recent IPV, tailored vs static (non-tailored) version of the same online tool
entries.finding: Both tailored and static/non-tailored arms improved significantly over time on depression (p<.001) and PTSD (p<.001) and on all secondary outcomes; changes did not differ significantly by study arm despite high self-reported benefit/safety/accessibility ratings in both groups.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates the assumption that tailoring/personalised scoring adds outcome benefit over a simpler static self-assessment tool - both versions worked equally well on primary mental-health outcomes, a relevant caution for how elaborate T-PHE's Layer 0 scoring needs to be.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms both arms improved significantly on depression (p<.001) and PTSD (p<.001) and all secondary outcomes, with no significant between-arm difference, and 'low risk of harm' in both groups. n=462 matches. Relevance claim (tailoring not required for benefit) is accurately caveated.

entries.title: Design and Development of a Suite of Intimate Partner Violence Screening and Safety Planning Web Apps: User-Centered Approach.
entries.design: User-centered design/development report (review)
entries.population_setting: Marginalized and vulnerable women, design collaboration with intended users, Canada
entries.finding: Describes user-centred/human-centred design of a suite of 3 app-based IPV screening and safety-planning tools, reporting design challenges and lessons for building mHealth/eHealth tools that let users control access to sensitive content.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports a user-centred, co-design approach for Layer 0's own scored self-check so results and routes are usable and safe for the target population, not just technically anonymous.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms user-centered/human-centered design of a suite of 3 app-based interventions and that they 'allow women to control access to these resources.' Correctly labeled as design/development report, not outcome data.

entries.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of iCanPlan: A Mobile Health Application for Intimate Partner Violence Prevention in Thailand.
entries.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
entries.design: Development + preliminary heuristic expert evaluation (n=30 multidisciplinary experts, 1-month use)
entries.population_setting: Thailand; IPV risk-assessment mobile app evaluated by gender-based-violence, social work, psychology, public health and NGO experts
entries.finding: Experts rated the app highly on usability (mean 4.93/5), safety features (4.73/5) and content quality (4.82/5), with perfect mean scores (5.00/5) for cultural appropriateness, language clarity, ethical considerations and overall evaluation; the app includes an IPV risk-assessment tool, a resource list and educational infographics.
entries.relevance_annotation: directly supports feasibility and cultural-appropriateness of a scored self-assessment IPV-prevention app in Thailand, the T-PHE setting itself, though evaluation is expert-only (not yet tested with the target population) - a gap the paper itself flags.
entries.verifier_note: The Thailand paper - checked with extra strictness given its centrality to T-PHE. All figures verified exactly: usability M=4.93, safety features M=4.73, content quality M=4.82, and perfect M=5.00 scores for cultural appropriateness/language clarity/ethical considerations/overall evaluation. n=30 multidisciplinary experts, 1-month use, confirmed. Abstract itself flags the gap the record notes: 'Further research involving the target population is needed to evaluate its effectiveness and long-term impact on help-seeking behavior and IPV-related outcomes.' Design is correctly described as expert heuristic evaluation, not an effectiveness trial - relevance claim does not overclaim beyond this.

entries.title: Empowering Safety: The Case for a Decision-making App for Military Partners Facing Intimate Partner Violence.
entries.design: Exploratory descriptive survey, single-site convenience sample, n=18
entries.evidence_level: descriptive/exploratory survey (low evidence level, explicitly hypothesis-generating)
entries.population_setting: Female service members and civilian partners, primary care clinic, Fort Bragg, North Carolina, USA
entries.finding: 9 of 18 participants reported IPV-related experiences in the previous 24 months; awareness/prior use of IPV apps was low, but 13 of 17 respondents expressed interest in a confidential decision-making/safety-support app; authors explicitly caution results are descriptive/hypothesis-generating only, from a small convenience sample.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports demand/acceptability for a confidential decision-support tool even where none currently exists, but at very low evidence level - a caution against overclaiming acceptability data from small convenience samples, relevant to T-PHE's own failure-criterion honesty.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=18, '9 of 18 participants reported IPV-related experiences during the previous 24 months', and '13 of 17 respondents expressed interest in a confidential, military-relevant IPV prevention or safety-support app', and explicitly: 'These findings should be interpreted as descriptive and hypothesis-generating.' Relevance claim correctly cautions against overclaiming from this small convenience sample.

entries.title: Computer-assisted screening for intimate partner violence and control: a randomized trial.
entries.design: Randomised trial, blinded outcome assessors, n=293 (144 intervention/149 control)
entries.population_setting: Adult women in a current/recent relationship, urban academic family practice clinic, Toronto, Canada
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Prevalence (22%, 95%CI 17-27%) and discussion-opportunity RR (1.4, CI 1.1-1.9, significant) verified exactly and support the relevance claim. But the 'increased detection of IPV' clause cites 'adjusted relative risk, 2.0 [CI, 0.9 to 4.1]' - this 95% CI crosses the null value of 1, so it is NOT statistically significant, even though both the source abstract and this record's key_finding present it as a confirmed increase. Correction: key_finding should note the detection-increase RR of 2.0 did not reach statistical significance (95% CI 0.9-4.1 spans 1); only the discussion-opportunity increase (RR 1.4, CI 1.1-1.9) is a confirmed significant effect.] Baseline prevalence of any IPV/control was 22% (95%CI 17-27%); computer-based self-report screening significantly increased opportunities to discuss IPV (adjusted RR 1.4, 95%CI 1.1-1.9). The adjusted RR for increased detection of IPV was 2.0 (95%CI 0.9-4.1), but this interval crosses the null value of 1 and is therefore not statistically significant.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] supports that a self-administered computer tool significantly increases opportunities to discuss IPV relative to unprompted clinical care (RR 1.4, CI 1.1-1.9); the reported increase in detection (RR 2.0) did not reach statistical significance and should not be cited as a confirmed detection benefit - an early foundational precedent for anonymous scored self-check mechanisms, on the discussion-opportunity outcome only.
entries.verifier_note: Prevalence (22%, 95%CI 17-27%) and discussion-opportunity RR (1.4, CI 1.1-1.9, significant) verified exactly and support the relevance claim. But the 'increased detection of IPV' clause cites 'adjusted relative risk, 2.0 [CI, 0.9 to 4.1]' - this 95% CI crosses the null value of 1, so it is NOT statistically significant, even though both the source abstract and this record's key_finding present it as a confirmed increase. Correction: key_finding should note the detection-increase RR of 2.0 did not reach statistical significance (95% CI 0.9-4.1 spans 1); only the discussion-opportunity increase (RR 1.4, CI 1.1-1.9) is a confirmed significant effect.

entries.title: Electronic Health Record-Based Screening for Intimate Partner Violence: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
entries.design: Stepped-wedge cluster RCT, 15 clinics, 8895 unique patients
entries.population_setting: Women 18-49y, family medicine primary care clinics, Charleston region, South Carolina, USA
entries.finding: Noninterruptive EHR alert plus confidential self-administered computer screening increased overall IPV screening rate from 45.2% (10,268/22,730 visits) to 65.3% (22,303/34,157 visits) (RR 1.46, 95%CI 1.44-1.49, p<.001); confidential self-screening detected past-year IPV in 1.5% (130/8895) of patients versus 0.1% (9/17,433) with nurse-led oral screening.
entries.relevance_annotation: strongly supports that a confidential, self-administered screening channel detects substantially more IPV than a face-to-face/oral route (15-fold higher detection), directly evidencing why Layer 0's anonymous self-held channel should outperform staff-mediated disclosure.
entries.verifier_note: All numbers verified exactly: screening rate 45.2% (10,268/22,730) to 65.3% (22,303/34,157), RR 1.46 (95%CI 1.44-1.49, p<.001); detection 1.5% (130/8895) vs 0.1% (9/17,433). 1.5/0.1=15, so the '15-fold higher detection' claim in relevance_to_tphe is arithmetically correct. Note for precision: this was a confidential EHR-linked computer screen tied to the patient's medical chart, not a fully anonymous unlinked self-check - relevance wording ('anonymous self-held channel') slightly blurs 'confidential' with 'anonymous'; consider tightening that word choice, though the core comparative-detection claim itself is fully supported.

entries.title: Risk for Severe Intimate Partner Violence in Nairobi's Informal Settlements: Tailoring the Danger Assessment to Kenya.
entries.design: Secondary prospective analysis of myPlan Kenya trial data
entries.population_setting: Women in 3 informal settlements, Nairobi, Kenya (LMIC)
entries.finding: A 16-item Kenya-adapted Danger Assessment (weighted) achieved sensitivity 66.67%, specificity 77.05%, C-statistic 0.78, and all Danger Assessment versions significantly predicted severe IPV at 3-month follow-up (original 20-item: OR 1.26, 95%CI 1.12-1.41).
entries.relevance_annotation: supports that a scored risk-assessment instrument can be validly tailored and can predict future severe violence in a non-Western LMIC context, relevant methodologically to how T-PHE's own scored self-check items would need local validation rather than direct import.
entries.verifier_note: All diagnostic statistics verified exactly: 16-item Kenya-DA weighted sensitivity 66.67%, specificity 77.05%, C-statistic 0.78; original 20-item DA OR=1.26 (95%CI 1.12-1.41, P<.001). Relevance claim correctly frames this as methodological support for local validation, not an efficacy transfer claim.

entries.title: Effectiveness of ICT-based intimate partner violence interventions: a systematic review.
entries.design: Systematic review, PRISMA, 25 included studies
entries.population_setting: Mixed - internet/mobile/smartphone IPV interventions, including LMIC settings
entries.finding: ICT-based interventions were found effective mainly for screening, disclosure and prevention; the review explicitly flags a lack of homogeneity in outcome measures, sample sizes and control conditions across studies, and notes unresolved questions on safety, equity and unintended consequences.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports the overall evidence base for technology-delivered IPV screening/self-assessment while explicitly flagging heterogeneity and unresolved safety/equity questions - directly relevant to honestly bounding T-PHE's own claims and failure criterion.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 25 included studies, effectiveness 'mainly in screening, disclosure, and prevention', and explicitly: 'Questions addressing safety, equity, and the unintended consequences of the use of ICT in IPV programming are virtually non-existent' - matches the key_finding's heterogeneity/unresolved-questions framing.

entries.title: Web-Based and mHealth Interventions for Intimate Partner Violence Victimization Prevention: A Systematic Review.
entries.design: Systematic review, 133 screened, 31 included studies, quality-appraised (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)
entries.population_setting: Adults in romantic relationships, mixed web-based and mHealth IPV prevention studies, 1998-2019
entries.finding: Computer-based screening with or without integrated education was the most common mHealth approach identified across the 31 included studies, spanning primary, secondary and tertiary IPV-victimisation prevention.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports self-administered computer-based screening as the dominant, established mHealth pattern for IPV prevention internationally, situating Layer 0's self-check within a well-precedented intervention class.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 133 screened / 31 included, and 'Computer-based screening with or without integrated education was the most common mHealth approach (n = 8, 26%), followed by safety decision aids (n = 7, 23%).' Relevance claim is a positioning claim (situates Layer 0 within a precedented intervention class), not an efficacy-transfer claim, so it is reasonable.

entries.title: Online Peer-to-Peer Support for Young People With Mental Health Problems: A Systematic Review
entries.design: systematic review (n=6 included studies)
entries.evidence_level: systematic review of primary studies (small n, mixed designs)
entries.population_setting: adolescents and young adults 12-25y, online peer-to-peer mental health support (Internet support groups, VR chat)
entries.finding: 6 studies met inclusion criteria; peer support was moderated by health professionals, researchers, or consumers in almost all (5/6) studies; only 2 of 3 RCTs showed a significant positive outcome vs control, the other 4 studies found no effect.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: mixed-to-weak effectiveness evidence for moderated peer support in this exact age band undercuts any claim Layer 3 will improve outcomes on its own; supports the design choice that moderation (not peer content alone) is the load-bearing safety feature, consistent with R4 routing.
entries.verifier_note: Ali K, JMIR Ment Health 2015, first author confirmed. Abstract: 'In almost all studies (n=5), the peer support intervention was moderated... two of the randomized controlled trials were associated with a significant positive outcome... In the remaining four studies, peer-to-peer support was not found to be effective.' Matches key_finding exactly.

entries.title: Understanding the Impacts of Online Mental Health Peer Support Forums: Realist Synthesis
entries.design: realist synthesis (102 evidence sources) + 18 stakeholder interviews with forum staff
entries.evidence_level: realist synthesis (program theory, not effectiveness trial)
entries.population_setting: online mental health peer support forum users and staff, published 2019-2023
entries.finding: Produced 22 context-mechanism-outcome configurations; psychological safety and content relevance drive engagement; moderators are described as vital to creating facilitative spaces and limiting distressing content; a key tension identified is balancing forum openness/anonymity against rule enforcement needed for community safety.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports: directly parallels T-PHE Layer 3's design tension (anonymous, peer-governed R2 channel vs moderator enforcement of no-partner-visible-content rules) and names moderator role as the mechanism that makes such forums work, not the peer interaction alone.
entries.verifier_note: Marshall P, JMIR Ment Health 2024. Abstract: 'produced an overarching program theory comprising 22 context-mechanism-outcome configurations... vital role of moderators... balancing forum openness and anonymity with the need to enforce rules.' Matches.

entries.title: Understanding Safety in Online Mental Health Forums: Realist Evaluation
entries.design: realist evaluation: 42 semistructured interviews + 504 cross-sectional survey responses
entries.evidence_level: realist evaluation, single-country (UK), self-report survey plus qualitative interviews
entries.population_setting: users of 3 UK-based online mental health forums (general, young-people-focused, eating disorder/postpartum psychosis subforums)
entries.finding: 40.1% agreed and 19.2% strongly agreed anonymity made them feel safe to post; but 18.8% agreed and 3.6% strongly agreed they had encountered distressing posts, and 22.4% agreed/3.4% strongly agreed that talking about mental health online could make them feel worse. Proactive content moderation and sensitive rule enforcement were identified as central safety mechanisms.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports and complicates simultaneously: quantifies real harm rates (~20-26% distress-related concerns) alongside the anonymity-enables-disclosure mechanism T-PHE's Layer 3/R2 relies on; the coexistence of benefit and measurable harm argues for the routing-not-mediation moderator role (R4) rather than assuming anonymity alone is protective.
entries.verifier_note: Marshall P, JMIR Ment Health 2025. Abstract percentages match exactly: '40.1% agreed and 19.2% strongly agreed' safe due to anonymity; '18.8% agreed and 3.6% strongly agreed' encountered distressing posts; '22.4% agreed... 3.4% strongly agreed' felt worse. UK-only sample, correctly scoped as such in evidence_level.

entries.title: Suicidal behaviours and moderator support in online health communities: a scoping review
entries.design: scoping review (5 studies included after screening 397 records)
entries.evidence_level: scoping review (very small evidence base, moderate-quality primary studies)
entries.population_setting: online forum moderators supporting individuals experiencing suicidal behaviour
entries.finding: Only 5 of 397 identified articles met inclusion criteria; only 1 article featured a moderator who was a qualified health professional, the rest were trained volunteers; evidence on moderators' professional working practices is described as sparse.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: exposes a large evidence gap on what moderators actually do in crisis situations, directly relevant to whether T-PHE's Layer 3 moderators (non-clinical, volunteer-style per the proposal) can safely route acute-risk disclosures rather than mediate them; underscores need for explicit escalation protocols, not assumed competence.
entries.verifier_note: Perry A, BMJ Open 2021. Abstract: '397 articles initially identified... five articles included for synthesis... Only one article featured a moderator who was a qualified health professional... dearth of research focusing on the professional practices of online forum moderators.' Matches.

entries.title: Barriers and enablers to the moderation of self-harm content for a young person's online forum
entries.design: qualitative interviews with 8 moderators (of 16 total) using the Behaviour Change Wheel
entries.evidence_level: qualitative study, single organisation (UK), n=8 moderators
entries.population_setting: moderators at The Mix, UK's leading online support service for people under 25
entries.finding: Thematic analysis identified 11 enablers, 4 barriers, and 1 element that was both, to moderating self-harm content; barriers included emotional exhaustion, working with partial information, and vague guidelines; a 'moderation buddy' social-support strategy was proposed.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports: directly informs the operational feasibility of T-PHE's moderator role for younger users; emotional exhaustion and vague guidelines are concrete implementation risks for a rule ('route, don't mediate') that this study shows is genuinely hard to apply consistently in practice.
entries.verifier_note: Perowne R, J Ment Health 2024. Abstract: 'Thematic analysis identified eleven enablers, four barriers and one both an enabler and a barrier. Barriers included emotional exhaustion, working with partial information... vagueness within the guidelines... a moderation buddy.' Matches.

entries.title: The Role of Moderators in Facilitating and Encouraging Peer-to-Peer Support in an Online Mental Health Community: A Qualitative Exploratory Study
entries.journal: Journal of Technology in Behavioral Science
entries.design: qualitative thematic content analysis, interviews with 20 moderators
entries.evidence_level: qualitative exploratory study, single platform, n=20 moderators
entries.population_setting: moderators ('Wall Guides') of the Togetherall online peer support platform
entries.finding: Moderators reported deep community connections and satisfaction from witnessing member progress, but also occasional aggressive, sensitive, or inconsiderate posts; response strategies included removing/revising posts, direct outreach to affected members, and consistent house-rule enforcement.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports: an operating example of exactly the R4 'route, don't mediate' distinction in practice, with named response tactics (remove content, reach out to individual, enforce shared rules) that T-PHE's Layer 3 could model directly.
entries.verifier_note: Deng D, J Technol Behav Sci 2023 (Togetherall 'Wall Guides', n=20). Abstract: 'They respond by removing or revising the hurtful post or reaching out to the affected member to maintain the house rules.' Directly supports the R4 route-not-mediate framing; not overstated.

entries.title: Safe spaces or toxic places? Content moderation and social dynamics of online eating disorder communities
entries.design: comparative computational analysis: 2.6M tweets (Twitter/X), 178K submissions (Reddit), 14K videos (TikTok), 2019-2023
entries.evidence_level: large-scale observational/computational content analysis (not causal experiment)
entries.population_setting: online eating-disorder discussion communities across three major platforms
entries.finding: Platforms with weaker moderation (Twitter/X) were found to enable toxic echo chambers that amplify pro-anorexia rhetoric, while more strongly moderated platforms did not show the same amplification pattern, despite similar user support-seeking behaviour across platforms.
entries.relevance_annotation: contradicts/complicates: direct evidence that a peer community without robust, consistently enforced moderation can amplify harm rather than reduce it, which is a specific warning against under-resourcing the moderator function in T-PHE's Layer 3.
entries.verifier_note: Lerman K, EPJ Data Sci 2025. Abstract: 'platforms with weaker moderation (like Twitter/X) enable the formation of toxic echo chambers that amplify pro-anorexia rhetoric.' This is a harms ANALOGY (eating-disorder communities, not IPV/premarital), and relevance_to_tphe correctly frames it as a 'specific warning' rather than IPV evidence -- appropriately hedged, no correction needed.

entries.title: How Cancer Online Support Groups Work, for Whom, and in What Circumstances: Realist Review
entries.design: realist review, 12 databases, 168 papers included from 16,659 identified
entries.population_setting: patients with cancer and cancer survivors using online support groups (OSGs)
entries.finding: OSGs can help via informational, emotional, appraisal, and altruistic support, but 'not all OSGs are helpful, and in some cases, they may increase distress'; positive outcomes depended on perceived trustworthiness, cultural safety, anonymity/privacy/control, and features such as moderation, norms, and group cohesion.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports and complicates: the largest and most recent realist synthesis of any online peer support group in this search explicitly states outcomes are context-dependent and can be harmful, reinforcing that T-PHE cannot assume Layer 3 will help by default and must engineer for the named enabling conditions (trust, anonymity/control, active moderation).
entries.verifier_note: Bender JL, J Med Internet Res 2026. Abstract quoted almost verbatim: "not all OSGs are helpful, and in some cases, they may increase distress"; outcomes depend on 'trustworthy... culturally safe'/'anonymity, privacy... autonomy'/'moderation, safety, cohesion'. Population is cancer patients -- an analogy, already correctly framed as such by the surrounding evidence_level note.

entries.title: Online Social Support for Intimate Partner Violence Victims in China: Quantitative and Automatic Content Analysis
entries.design: quantitative + automatic (machine-learning) content analysis of 90,040 messages (8,343 hand-coded subset)
entries.evidence_level: observational content analysis, single platform/country, no outcome measure of victim wellbeing
entries.population_setting: a popular Chinese online community's IPV discussion group
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Chu TH, Violence Against Women 2021, China IPV community. key_finding is supported: abstract states 'social support is commonly presented, while only a few messages expressed blame toward the victims... a space for the victims to obtain informational resources and emotional encouragement.' BUT relevance_to_tphe overreaches on two points: (1) it asserts the community was 'unmoderated-by-default' -- the abstract says nothing about moderation status, this is an unsupported inference; (2) it generalizes a single Chinese platform to an 'Asian cultural context' -- per the task's own instruction, a Chinese peer community is not Thai, and should not be broadened to 'Asian.' FIX: delete the 'unmoderated-by-default' claim and replace 'Asian cultural context' with 'China-specific, offered only as a non-Western analogy -- not evidence for a Thai or Muslim-majority setting.'] Social support was commonly present in messages; only a small minority of messages expressed victim-blaming; the community functioned as a source of informational resources and emotional encouragement for IPV victims.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] supports: empirical, non-Western evidence that a peer community around IPV/relationship harm can generate predominantly supportive (not blaming) content; the abstract does not state the community's moderation status, so no claim about being unmoderated-by-default is made. This is China-specific, offered only as a non-Western analogy - not evidence for a Thai or Muslim-majority setting.
entries.verifier_note: Chu TH, Violence Against Women 2021, China IPV community. key_finding is supported: abstract states 'social support is commonly presented, while only a few messages expressed blame toward the victims... a space for the victims to obtain informational resources and emotional encouragement.' BUT relevance_to_tphe overreaches on two points: (1) it asserts the community was 'unmoderated-by-default' -- the abstract says nothing about moderation status, this is an unsupported inference; (2) it generalizes a single Chinese platform to an 'Asian cultural context' -- per the task's own instruction, a Chinese peer community is not Thai, and should not be broadened to 'Asian.' FIX: delete the 'unmoderated-by-default' claim and replace 'Asian cultural context' with 'China-specific, offered only as a non-Western analogy -- not evidence for a Thai or Muslim-majority setting.'

entries.title: Effectiveness of ICT-based intimate partner violence interventions: a systematic review
entries.design: systematic review following PRISMA, 25 studies included
entries.evidence_level: systematic review (PRISMA), moderate methodological heterogeneity noted by authors
entries.population_setting: women exposed to IPV, ICT-based interventions (internet, mobile, web, ehealth)
entries.finding: ICT-based interventions were effective mainly for screening, disclosure, and prevention; the review found questions of safety, equity, and unintended consequences of ICT use in IPV programming were 'virtually non-existent' in the literature, and only one study formally assessed software usability.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: a systematic review explicitly flags that safety/unintended-consequences research for digital IPV tools is almost absent, which is a direct evidence gap T-PHE's Layer 3 (a digital peer channel touching relationship-safety topics) would need to address rather than assume away.
entries.verifier_note: El Morr C, BMC Public Health 2020. Abstract: 'Questions addressing safety, equity, and the unintended consequences of the use of ICT in IPV programming are virtually non-existent... only one study formally addressed software usability.' Matches quote precisely, including the 'virtually non-existent' quote.

entries.title: Intimate partner violence: a review of online interventions
entries.design: scoping review, literature 2000-2016, 11 interventions identified
entries.evidence_level: scoping review, literature pre-2017 (dated relative to current social media landscape)
entries.population_setting: women in the context of intimate partner violence, online interventions
entries.finding: Existing online IPV interventions focused mainly on the act of leaving an abusive relationship, with limited emphasis on post-departure needs or the broader social-contextual factors of IPV; findings highlighted information gaps for women needing support after leaving.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: suggests existing digital IPV support tools have a narrow scope (leaving-focused) that a peer community layer like T-PHE's would need to deliberately widen (post-separation, ongoing relationship-safety) rather than replicate the same gap.
entries.verifier_note: Rempel E, Inform Health Soc Care 2019. Abstract: 'online interventions focused on the act of leaving with less emphasis on the experiences that occur after a woman has left the relationship... findings highlight information gaps for women who require significant support after leaving.' Matches.

entries.title: Technology-Facilitated Abuse in Intimate Relationships: A Scoping Review
entries.design: scoping review, MEDLINE/CINAHL/Scopus, 22 studies (2000-2020), UK/Ireland/US/Canada/NZ/Australia
entries.evidence_level: scoping review, English-speaking high-income countries only
entries.population_setting: adults 18+ in intimate partnerships experiencing technology-facilitated abuse (TFA)
entries.finding: TFA is diverse and maps onto all eight domains of the Duluth Power & Control Wheel (surveillance apps, spyware, social media misuse etc.); impacts span social, mental-health, and financial harm plus a described sense of 'omnipresence'; victim/survivor resistance was infrequently reported and mainly involved direct action or professional/legal support.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports the harms angle directly: names the specific mechanism by which a digital peer/relationship channel can itself become a vector of partner surveillance and control, which is exactly what T-PHE's 'no partner-visible content' rule (R2) is designed to defend against.
entries.verifier_note: Rogers MM, Trauma Violence Abuse 2023. Abstract: 'TFA is diverse... can be typed according to the eight domains of the Duluth Power & Control Wheel... social, mental health and financial impacts and omnipresence... modes of resistance are infrequently reported.' Matches; evidence_level correctly scopes to English-speaking high-income countries.

entries.title: Technology-Facilitated Domestic and Sexual Violence: A Review
entries.design: narrative review
entries.population_setting: adult women experiencing domestic and sexual violence via digital communications technologies
entries.finding: Describes empirical literature on digital dating abuse, intimate partner cyberstalking, technology-facilitated sexual assault, image-based sexual abuse, and online sexual harassment as a growing, interconnected problem requiring gendered conceptual frameworks.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports the harms angle: establishes that the same digital channels a peer-support layer would use (messaging, social platforms) are documented vectors for partner abuse, reinforcing the necessity of T-PHE's anonymous-by-choice and no-partner-visible-content design.
entries.verifier_note: Henry N, Violence Against Women 2020 (narrative review, solo/lead author). Abstract confirms coverage of digital dating abuse, intimate partner cyberstalking, technology-facilitated sexual assault, image-based sexual abuse, online sexual harassment, and call for gendered frameworks. Matches.

entries.title: Technology-Facilitated Domestic Violence Against Immigrant and Refugee Women: A Qualitative Study
entries.design: qualitative study, interviews with 29 victim-survivors and 20 stakeholders
entries.evidence_level: qualitative study, single-country (Australia), not generalizable numerically
entries.population_setting: immigrant and refugee women experiencing technology-facilitated domestic violence (TFDV), Australia
entries.finding: Immigrant/refugee women face TFDV similarly to other women but with added unique barriers: language, cultural bias from services, limited financial resources, low trust in state institutions, and additional justice/migration-system obstacles.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: raises a population-specific equity concern (migrant/minority status, language, institutional distrust) that a moderated digital peer community serving diverse Thai/Muslim populations should anticipate rather than assume uniform safety/trust across users.
entries.verifier_note: Henry N (co-authored), J Interpersonal Violence 2022, Australia. Abstract: 'unique challenges, such as language barriers, cultural bias from support services, lack of financial resources, lack of trust in state institutions, and additional challenges with justice and migration systems.' Matches; interview counts (29 victim-survivors, 20 stakeholders) match exactly.

entries.title: Cyberstalking Perpetrators and Their Methods: A Systematic Literature Review
entries.design: systematic literature review, SCOPUS and Web of Science, 80 articles included
entries.evidence_level: systematic review, mixed empirical study designs and quality
entries.population_setting: cyberstalking perpetrators (general population studies)
entries.finding: Perpetrators were characterised by poor social skills, low self-control, prior physical-abuse victimization, stalking-related attitudes, and higher internet use; common motives were relationship reconciliation, revenge, or establishing control; most frequent methods were unwanted repeated contact, account access, GPS tracking, and impersonation online.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports the harms angle: names concrete cyberstalking methods (account access, GPS tracking, impersonation, unwanted contact via the same platforms) directly relevant to why T-PHE's Layer 3 must be designed so a partner cannot surveil or access a learner's peer-community activity.
entries.verifier_note: Weekes CJ, Trauma Violence Abuse 2026. Abstract: perpetrators 'lack social skills, have low self-control, have experienced physical abuse victimization... motivated by trying to reconcile a relationship, exact revenge... methods... accessing the victim's accounts, tracking their GPS location, posing as the victim online.' Matches.

entries.title: Post-separation Parenting Apps as Tools for Control and Resistance
entries.design: qualitative study, interviews with 18 separated mothers
entries.evidence_level: qualitative study, small sample (n=18), single-country context
entries.population_setting: mothers coparenting post-separation with a domestic-violence perpetrator, using court-recommended communication apps
entries.finding: Record-keeping functions built into coparenting apps (intended for accountability) were shown to function as sites where coercive control is both exercised and resisted, shaped by the legal context that mandated the apps' use.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: a cautionary parallel showing that a technology explicitly designed to be safe/accountable can still be repurposed for control by an abusive partner, a direct design-risk lesson for any T-PHE feature (records, logs) touching relationship communication.
entries.verifier_note: Irving M, Violence Against Women 2026 (n=18 separated mothers). Abstract: 'The record-keeping functions of these apps emerged as a key mechanism through which both control and resistance are negotiated, shaped by the legal settings in which app use is often introduced.' Matches.

entries.title: Self-disclosure versus self-presentation on social media
entries.design: narrative review of the literature on medium characteristics and online self-disclosure
entries.population_setting: general social media users
entries.finding: Anonymity and reduced information richness were identified as factors that increase self-disclosure, while asynchronicity, multiple audiences, and audience feedback were identified as factors favoring self-presentation (impression management) instead of genuine disclosure.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: identifies structural features of online spaces (audience visibility, feedback dynamics) that can push users toward curated self-presentation rather than honest disclosure, a caveat for assuming anonymity alone in T-PHE's Layer 3 guarantees candid peer consultation.
entries.verifier_note: Schlosser AE, Curr Opin Psychol 2020. Abstract: 'anonymity and reduced information richness... argued to increase self-disclosure... asynchronicity, multiple audiences, and audience feedback... favor self-presentation.' Matches exactly.

entries.title: Disclosure in psychotherapy versus in anonymous and non-anonymous online spaces
entries.design: cross-sectional online survey, N=443
entries.population_setting: heterogeneous adult sample comparing disclosure in therapy vs. anonymous/non-anonymous online spaces
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Mayopoulos G, Psychother Res 2024 (N=443), first author and design confirmed. The first sentence of key_finding is supported: 'attachment style plays a significant role in determining individuals' likelihood of discussing personally distressing topics online... and in anonymous and non-anonymous online spaces to be helpful.' BUT the second clause inverts the abstract's actual claim. Search file says: 'younger patients and those with avoidant/ambivalent attachment styles were flagged as more likely to view ONLINE DISCLOSURE as an appropriate venue.' Abstract actually says the opposite object: clinicians should check whether such patients 'view PSYCHOTHERAPY as an appropriate domain to disclose specific personally distressful issues' -- i.e. the flag is about whether they see therapy (not online spaces) as legitimate. FIX: replace with 'clinicians are advised to monitor whether younger patients and those with avoidant/ambivalent attachment styles view psychotherapy itself as an appropriate venue for disclosure, given their documented tendency to disclose online instead.'] Attachment style significantly predicted likelihood of disclosing distressing topics online and whether disclosures in therapy vs. anonymous/non-anonymous online spaces were experienced as helpful; clinicians are advised to monitor whether younger patients and those with avoidant/ambivalent attachment styles view psychotherapy itself as an appropriate venue for disclosure, given their documented tendency to disclose online instead.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] supports and complicates: gives an individual-differences mechanism (attachment style) for why 'younger people treat digital spaces as safer' is not uniformly true, and flags that clinicians should monitor whether such patients still see psychotherapy (the professional venue) as legitimate, given their tendency to disclose online instead - by extension a caution for T-PHE's moderators not to assume online disclosure substitutes for professional venues.

BUT the second clause inverts the abstract's actual claim. entries.title: Young People's Online Help-Seeking and Mental Health Difficulties: Systematic Narrative Review
entries.design: systematic narrative review (PRISMA), 28 studies included
entries.evidence_level: systematic narrative review (PRISMA), moderate-to-strong quality primary studies
entries.population_setting: young people seeking help online for mental health difficulties
entries.finding: Key benefits of online help-seeking were anonymity/privacy, immediacy, ease of access, inclusivity, connection with others, and greater sense of control; barriers included low mental health literacy, privacy/confidentiality concerns, and uncertainty about trustworthiness of online resources; limited theoretical frameworks have been applied to online help-seeking.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports: the closest direct evidence for the proposal's stated assumption that younger people find digital spaces safer/more accessible for help-seeking, while also naming trust/credibility barriers relevant to how T-PHE's Layer 3 should be governed and presented.
entries.verifier_note: Pretorius C, J Med Internet Res 2019 (28 studies, PRISMA). Abstract: 'Key benefits included anonymity and privacy, immediacy, ease of access, inclusivity... a greater sense of control... Barriers to help-seeking included a lack of mental health literacy, concerns about privacy and confidentiality, and uncertainty about the trustworthiness of online resources.' Matches.

entries.title: Social Media and Online Digital Technology Use Among Muslim Young People and Parents: Qualitative Focus Group Study
entries.design: qualitative participatory study, focus groups with 33 young people (16-22y) and 15 parents (40-57y)
entries.evidence_level: qualitative focus-group study, single city/country, not Thailand-specific
entries.population_setting: Muslim young people and parents, Melbourne, Australia
entries.finding: Social media served as an important extension of social/cultural/religious connection, especially during COVID-19; young participants used it to build identity and belonging, but also faced discrimination and unrealistic beauty/success standards online; a large digital divide existed between young people's and parents' online experiences and concerns.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports and complicates: the only Muslim-community-specific record found; supports that digital spaces can serve identity/belonging/community-connection functions relevant to T-PHE's target population, but also documents discrimination exposure as a harm and a parent-youth digital-divide relevant to family-context governance of Layer 3.
entries.verifier_note: Douglass CH, JMIR Pediatr Parent 2022, Melbourne Australia (33 young people 16-22y, 15 parents). Abstract: 'social media was an important extension of social and cultural connections, particularly during COVID-19... young participants perceived social media as a space where they could establish their identity and feel a sense of belonging. However, participants were also at risk of being exposed to discrimination...' Matches. relevance_to_tphe and evidence_level both correctly flag this as Australia, not Thailand-specific -- consistent with gaps_noted.

entries.title: The Independent Living Donor Advocate: An Essential Role for Living Kidney Donation.
entries.design: Narrative/policy review
entries.population_setting: US living kidney donor transplant programs (post-2007 CMS/UNOS regulation)
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Abstract quote: 'Transplant programs must now have an advocate or advocate team who is separate from the recipient healthcare team to provide objective support for the donor, without regard for the recipient, and avoid any perception of a conflict of interest between the donor and recipient.' Key finding is accurate. But this is a transplant-medicine record; per checker instructions such records are ANALOGIES and must never be phrased as 'supports'. relevance_to_tphe currently opens with 'supports R4 no-stake assessor' — FIX by rewording to 'analogous to R4 no-stake assessor (transplant-medicine analogy, not domain-matched)'.] Post-2007 US regulation requires transplant programs to appoint an independent living donor advocate or advocate team, structurally separate from the recipient's care team, specifically to avoid any perception of conflict of interest between donor and recipient.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] analogy (non-domain-matched) to R4 no-stake assessor: transplant-medicine analogy — regulator-mandated separation of the person assessing/protecting the vulnerable party from the team with a stake in the transaction proceeding.
