entries.title: The Psychosocial and Independent Living Donor Advocate Evaluation and Post-surgery Care of Living Donors.
entries.journal: Journal of Clinical Psychology in Medical Settings
entries.design: Narrative/policy review
entries.population_setting: US live organ donor transplant programs
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Abstract confirms CMS/UNOS-mandated ILDA evaluation, separated from transplant candidate's team, covering informed consent and psychosocial evaluation, e.g. 'Two areas in which had significant changes included the psychosocial and the independent living donor advocate (ILDA) evaluation.' Key finding accurate ('voluntariness of donation' is a fair paraphrase of the informed-consent/education content). Same issue as 26287054: transplant-medicine analogy currently phrased as 'supports R4' — FIX to explicit analogy language.] Describes CMS/UNOS-mandated independent donor advocate evaluation process, separated from the transplant candidate's team, covering informed consent, psychosocial evaluation and voluntariness of donation.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] analogy (non-domain-matched) to R4 no-stake assessor: transplant-medicine analogy — shows a regulated, standardized process for keeping evaluation of a vulnerable party's welfare separate from the professionals who benefit from the procedure occurring.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms CMS/UNOS-mandated ILDA evaluation, separated from transplant candidate's team, covering informed consent and psychosocial evaluation, e.g. 'Two areas in which had significant changes included the psychosocial and the independent living donor advocate (ILDA) evaluation.' entries.title: Ethical Analysis and Policy Recommendations Regarding Domino Liver Transplantation.
entries.design: Ethical analysis / case-based policy proposal
entries.population_setting: Domino liver donor transplant candidates (pediatric case example)
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Abstract quote: 'We propose a Domino Donor Advocate-based on the concept of the independent living donor advocate... We discuss the need for 2 distinct consent processes separated in time to ensure that potential domino donors... give a truly voluntary consent.' Key finding accurate. Transplant-medicine analogy again phrased as 'supports R4 no-stake assessor and P5 referral timing' — FIX to analogy language per instructions.] Proposes a 'Domino Donor Advocate', modeled explicitly on the independent living donor advocate, plus two consent processes separated in time, to protect voluntariness when the same party stands to gain from securing consent.
entries.relevance_annotation: [read with the correction above] analogy (non-domain-matched) to R4 no-stake assessor and P5 referral timing (separated processes before the day): transplant-medicine analogy — reinforces that a party with a stake in an irreversible transaction should not be the one certifying voluntariness/safety.

We discuss the need for 2 distinct consent processes separated in time to ensure that potential domino donors... give a truly voluntary consent.' Key finding accurate. Transplant-medicine analogy again phrased as 'supports R4 no-stake assessor and P5 referral timing' — FIX to analogy language per instructions.

entries.title: Ethics and the facial plastic surgeon.
entries.design: Narrative ethics review
entries.population_setting: Facial plastic/cosmetic surgery practice
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: Abstract quote: 'The facial plastic surgeon potentially has a conflict of interest when confronted with the patients requesting surgery, due to the personal gain attainable by agreeing to perform surgery.' entries.title: Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media.
entries.design: 7 preregistered studies: 6 RCTs (n=6464) + 1 ecologically valid field study on YouTube (n=22,632)
entries.population_setting: General adult social-media users, online panels + YouTube ad viewers
entries.finding: Five short videos inoculating against manipulation techniques (emotionally manipulative language, incoherence, false dichotomies, scapegoating, ad hominem) improved manipulation-technique recognition, boosted confidence in spotting techniques, increased discernment of trustworthy vs untrustworthy content, and improved quality of sharing decisions, across n=6464 (RCTs) and n=22,632 (field).
entries.relevance_annotation: supports: Layer 0 awareness mechanism -- direct causal evidence that brief exposure to the pattern of a manipulation technique (not the specific deceptive content itself) raises subsequent independent recognition of that technique in new material. This is the closest existing PubMed-indexed evidence for the author's core claim that 'recognising the pattern once' confers resistance. Caveat: domain is media/political misinformation, not interpersonal coercive-relationship manipulation -- an analogy, not a direct transplant.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms: 'these videos improve manipulation technique recognition, boost confidence in spotting these techniques, increase people's ability to discern trustworthy from untrustworthy content, and improve the quality of their sharing decisions' across 6 RCTs (n=6464) + YouTube field study (n=22,632). Correctly measures technique recognition (not belief in a specific claim). relevance_to_tphe already labels this an analogy across domains. No changes needed.

entries.title: Can Attitudes Serve as Proxies for Behavioral Outcomes of Dating Violence Prevention Programs? Broader Lessons From a Pilot Evaluation of the Relationship Education Project.
entries.design: Pre-post pilot evaluation, students in 19 middle/high schools, South Carolina
entries.population_setting: US middle/high-school students, teen dating violence (TDV) prevention programme
entries.finding: Favorable pre-post changes in attitudes toward controlling vs supportive dating behaviors were associated with lower incidence of some subsequent TDV behaviors, but the paper explicitly flags that attitude/knowledge change (the outcome type closest to 'recognition') has limited demonstrated correspondence to actual behavioral prevention across the wider literature.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: directly relevant failure-criterion evidence -- this is exactly the caution T-PHE's Layer 0 claim needs to sit against: recognition/attitude-change outcomes are a weak, imperfect proxy for actual behavioral protection, so 'people recognised the pattern' cannot alone be equated with 'people were protected from manipulation'. Use to bound the awareness-protects claim, not to inflate it.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms: 'favorable changes in attitudes toward controlling and supportive dating behaviors were associated with lower incidents of some TDV behaviors' and explicitly frames the broader literature gap ('limited evidence of meaningful effects on behavior' from attitude/knowledge proxies). key_finding and relevance_to_tphe (used as a 'complicates' bounding caution) match. entries.title: One-year follow-up of a coach-delivered dating violence prevention program: a cluster randomized controlled trial.
entries.design: Cluster RCT, 16 high schools, N=1513 male athletes, 12-month follow-up
entries.population_setting: US high-school male athletes (Grades 9-11), 'Coaching Boys Into Men' bystander-based dating-violence prevention
entries.finding: [CORRECTION: MAJOR ERROR. Current key_finding claims the programme 'showed longer-term (1-year) effects on bystander intervention behaviors' framed as a positive recognition/prevention result. The abstract's actual RESULTS directly contradict this: 'No differences were observed in intentions to intervene...; recognition of abusive behaviors (-0.03, 95% CI=-0.15, 0.09); or positive bystander behaviors (0.04, 95% CI=-0.11, 0.19).' The only significant effects were on reduced PERPETRATION (-0.15, 95% CI=-0.27,-0.03) and reduced NEGATIVE bystander behaviors i.e. laughing/going along with abuse (-0.41, 95% CI=-0.72,-0.10) -- not on recognition or positive bystander intervention. This is exactly the kind of record the T-PHE authors need most: a rigorous cluster RCT in which the recognition outcome specifically FAILED to show a 1-year effect, even though downstream behavior (perpetration) did improve -- i.e. dissociates 'recognition changed' from 'behavior changed', the opposite pattern from what the current key_finding implies. Verdict must flip from 'supports' to 'complicates'. CORRECTED key_finding to write back: "In a 12-month follow-up of a cluster RCT (16 high schools, N=1513 male athletes), Coaching Boys Into Men (a coach-delivered dating violence prevention programme) showed NO significant 1-year effect on its primary recognition-of-abusive-behaviors outcome (-0.03, 95% CI=-0.15,0.09), intentions to intervene, gender-equitable attitudes, or positive bystander behaviors (0.04, 95% CI=-0.11,0.19). It DID show significant reductions in dating violence perpetration (-0.15, 95% CI=-0.27,-0.03) and in negative bystander behaviors i.e. laughing along with peers' abusive behaviors (-0.41, 95% CI=-0.72,-0.10)." This is strong caution against assuming 'improved recognition' is either necessary or the active ingredient behind any behavioral protection a programme like Layer 0 might eventually show -- recognition and protective behavior change appear here as separable, not automatically coupled, outcomes."] In a 12-month follow-up of a cluster RCT (16 high schools, N=1513 male athletes), Coaching Boys Into Men (a coach-delivered dating violence prevention programme) showed NO significant 1-year effect on its primary recognition-of-abusive-behaviors outcome (-0.03, 95% CI=-0.15,0.09), intentions to intervene, gender-equitable attitudes, or positive bystander behaviors (0.04, 95% CI=-0.11,0.19). entries.title: Being silenced, loneliness and being heard: understanding pathways to intimate partner violence & abuse in young adults. a mixed-methods study.

entries.evidence_level: Mixed-methods, includes large longitudinal cohort component (ALSPAC)
entries.population_setting: UK young adults (ALSPAC birth cohort)
entries.finding: Qualitative pathways to intimate partner violence and abuse (IPVA) centred on themes of being silenced and unheard; quantitative arm modelled associations between earlier childhood factors (e.g., maltreatment) and later IPVA experience in a large longitudinal cohort.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports (population-level pathway context): situates recognition/voice as one node in a larger pathway toward IPVA vulnerability in young adults, i.e. awareness/being-heard is embedded in a wider causal web (childhood factors, social context) -- useful to avoid T-PHE overclaiming that awareness alone is sufficient; awareness is one lever among several upstream/downstream factors.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms qualitative pathway themes (being silenced/unheard, negative labelling) and the ALSPAC quantitative arm (child maltreatment -> adolescent loneliness -> young-adult IPVA, with loneliness mediating). Ns (17 women; 2127 female/1145 male ALSPAC) match. relevance_to_tphe's 'awareness is one lever among several' framing matches the abstract's mediation-pathway structure. No changes needed.

entries.title: Disclosure and Help-Seeking Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minority Victims of Intimate Partner Violence: A Mixed-Methods Study.
entries.design: Mixed-methods, semi-structured interviews with N=41 SGM-AFAB young adults who experienced physical, sexual, or severe psychological IPV
entries.population_setting: US sexual and gender minority young adults assigned female at birth
entries.finding: Three-quarters of participants disclosed their IPV experience to someone; disclosure/help-seeking rates and helpfulness of responses varied by demographic subgroup and relationship to the person disclosed to, revealing structural and social barriers specific to this population.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports (angle c, help-seeking after recognition): directly evidences that even after IPV is experienced, disclosure/help-seeking is not automatic and depends on population-specific barriers -- relevant to T-PHE's implicit assumption that recognition leads onward to protective action; recognition (labelling something as abuse) is necessary but the abstract does not establish it is sufficient for help-seeking.
entries.verifier_note: N=41 SGM-AFAB, three-quarters disclosed, variation by demographic/relationship-to-discloser -- all confirmed in abstract. Note for context (not an error, just an underused strengthening point): the abstract's most common disclosure barrier was 'not viewing the IPV as abuse' -- i.e. failure to recognize is literally named as the top barrier, which would make the relevance_to_tphe case for Layer 0 even stronger than currently written, but the existing text is not inaccurate, so left as-is (KEEP, not FIX) rather than rewriting a correct-but-conservative claim.

entries.title: Further psychometric examination of the Intimate Partner Violence Internalized Stigma Scale (IPVIS; Brunton & Harris, 2023): Examining criterion-related validity.
entries.design: Psychometric/instrument-validation study
entries.population_setting: IPV-victimized individuals (scale-validation sample)
entries.finding: Provides further criterion-related validity evidence for the IPVIS, a scale measuring IPV self-stigma (awareness of and internalized agreement with negative IPV stereotypes), which the paper explicitly frames as a barrier to help-seeking, distinct from recognition of the abuse itself.
entries.relevance_annotation: complicates: a caution/failure-criterion node -- even where recognition of coercive/abusive dynamics occurs, internalized stigma about being a 'victim' is a separately measured construct that can itself block help-seeking; T-PHE's Layer 0 (recognition) does not by itself address this downstream stigma barrier, so 'recognised the pattern' is necessary but not sufficient evidence of protection or of an unblocked path to support.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms IPVIS measures 'awareness of and agreeance with negative IPV stereotypes/attitudes... internalized by individuals victimized by IPV', framed as a help-seeking barrier distinct from abuse recognition itself. key_finding and relevance_to_tphe (recognition necessary-but-not-sufficient caution) match. No changes needed.

entries.title: Generic Health Literacy Measurements for Adults: A Scoping Review.
entries.journal: International journal of environmental research and public health
entries.design: Scoping review, 19 identified generic health literacy measurement instruments
entries.population_setting: Adults, generic (non-disease-specific) health literacy instruments across the literature
entries.finding: Identifies 19 generic health literacy measures; most apply a multidimensional definition centred on individuals' abilities to access, appraise, understand, and apply health information and services, with Nutbeam's conceptual model and Sørensen's integrated model as the two most widely used theoretical foundations.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports (angle d, health-literacy model): confirms the 'access -> understand -> appraise -> apply' (Sørensen) and Nutbeam multidimensional health-literacy frameworks are the field's established theoretical scaffolding, which T-PHE's Layer 0 self-check/signal-recognition design can be explicitly mapped onto (recognition = the appraise stage) rather than inventing a bespoke construct; general health literacy, not relationship-safety-specific.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 19 measures identified, Nutbeam and Sørensen models as dominant theoretical foundations, multidimensional access/appraise/understand/apply framing. key_finding and relevance_to_tphe (mapping recognition onto the 'appraise' stage) match. No changes needed.

entries.title: One Size Doesn't Fit All: Dating Abuse Against Women From the Perspective of South Asian Muslim Youth in Canada.
entries.design: Exploratory qualitative study, N=11 South Asian Muslim participants
entries.population_setting: South Asian Muslim youth, Canada (diaspora)
entries.finding: Participants identified four culturally distinct domains in which South Asian Muslim women may experience/understand dating abuse differently: exposure to parents/community, sexual-nature behaviors, controlling behaviors, and psychological/emotional/verbal abuse -- supporting an intersectionality perspective on how recognition of abuse is culturally shaped.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports (angle e, Muslim-context evidence): directly relevant to T-PHE's target population framing -- shows recognition of psychological/controlling abuse is not culturally universal but is filtered through community/family exposure norms specific to South Asian Muslim contexts, meaning a generic (Western) 'signals' checklist may need cultural adaptation to be recognisable/legible to a Muslim-Thai audience. Small qualitative sample (N=11), not generalisable on its own.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms N=11, four domains (parents/community exposure, sexual-nature behaviors, controlling behaviors, psychological/emotional/verbal abuse) and the intersectionality framing. key_finding and relevance_to_tphe (cultural-adaptation caution for a Muslim-diaspora audience, small-N caveat) match. No changes needed.

entries.title: Reflections on attitudes, experiences, and vulnerability of intimate partner violence among Southeast Asian college women living in United States.
entries.design: Qualitative focus-group study, N=18 Southeast Asian college women, ages 18-34
entries.population_setting: Southeast Asian diaspora college women in the United States
entries.finding: Five themes emerged: recognition of IPV, perception of individual vulnerability to IPV, experience/responses to IPV, help-seeking and support system, and prevention strategies -- with cultural norms shown to shape both recognition of IPV and willingness to seek help.
entries.relevance_annotation: supports (angle e, Southeast Asian evidence): closest population-adjacent PubMed record to T-PHE's own target demographic; explicitly names 'recognition of IPV' as its own distinct, separately-themed construct from help-seeking, and shows both are shaped by Southeast Asian cultural norms -- supports treating Layer 0 recognition and Layer-onward help-seeking as related but analytically separate outcome domains for T-PHE's programme theory. Small qualitative sample (N=18), US diaspora not Thailand-resident population.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms N=18, five themes (recognition of IPV, perceived vulnerability, experience/responses, help-seeking/support, prevention strategies) and a general cultural-norms discussion. key_finding matches closely; relevance_to_tphe's specific 'shapes both recognition and willingness to seek help' framing is a fair paraphrase of the abstract's broader 'intertwined cultural norms... challenges for IPV prevention' statement, not a verbatim overclaim. No changes needed.

entries.title: Humility, Forgiveness, and Emerging Adult Female Romantic Relationships
entries.journal: Journal of marital and family therapy
entries.design: cross-sectional survey, serial mediation path analysis
entries.evidence_level: cross-sectional, single sample, path-analytic mediation (not RCT/longitudinal)
entries.population_setting: emerging adult women, N=152, US convenience sample, currently in a romantic relationship
entries.finding: Perceived humility related to relationship satisfaction via a serial mediation path through self-forgiveness then partner-forgiveness (N=152); effect not reducible to impression management.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports R1 humility as a construct with measured downstream relational benefit (forgiveness -> satisfaction). Directly on the acknowledging one's own limits/humility node of T-PHE's sequence, though this is a psychological trait-humility study, not a religious-ethics study; the theological chain (acknowledging one's own limits->conscientious self-restraint->entrusted responsibility) is an analogy T-PHE draws, not something this paper tests.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'humility was related to relationship satisfaction via a serially mediated path of self-forgiveness and partner-forgiveness, which was not reducible to impression management.' N=152 matches. Relevance framing correctly labels this a psychological trait-humility study, not a theological test of T-PHE's chain.

entries.title: Intellectual humility is reliably associated with constructive responses to conflict
entries.design: two-study correlational/survey design (interpersonal and workplace conflict contexts)
entries.population_setting: general adult samples, Study 1 (friends/family conflict) and Study 2 (workplace conflict)
entries.finding: Intellectual humility (awareness of one's own fallibility) predicted more constructive and less destructive responses to conflict across both interpersonal and workplace conflict contexts, replicated across two studies.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports R1 humility and mechanism 'decision control': humility as awareness of fallibility maps onto T-PHE's acknowledging one's own limits construct and its claimed effect on conflict-handling behaviour is the closest PubMed-indexed analogue to the humility->conscientious-restraint link T-PHE proposes; still an analogy, since T-PHE's sequence is normative/ethical, this evidence is descriptive/associational.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'intellectual humility predicts more constructive and less destructive responses to conflict' across Study 1 (friends/family) and Study 2 (workplace). Correctly described as correlational, no intervention.

entries.title: Intellectual Humility Predicts Empathic Accuracy and Empathic Resilience
entries.design: three preregistered studies (two correlational, one experimental manipulation) with mini meta-analysis
entries.evidence_level: experimental (manipulation study within a three-study design) plus mini meta-analysis; general adult population, not premarital/health-education context
entries.population_setting: general adult samples, N=533 total across three studies (n=212, n=112, n=209)
entries.finding: Intellectual humility (IH) positively associated with empathic accuracy (mini meta-analysis across studies), especially toward outgroup members; experimentally manipulated increases in state IH were associated with greater empathic accuracy; IH also predicted empathic resilience (buffering personal distress while maintaining empathic concern).
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports R1 humility -> R3-adjacent openness/perspective-taking mechanism: humility causally (via manipulation) increasing empathic accuracy is evidence that a humility-based safeguard could plausibly support the compassion/openness-to-correction chain T-PHE assumes; complicates any claim of a specific effect size for T-PHE itself, since this is general-population evidence, not evidence for T-PHE's programme.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: N=533 (n=212, n=112, n=209) matches exactly; 'positive association between IH and empathic accuracy... especially toward the outgroup'; Study 3 manipulation 'to demonstrate causality'; IH also predicted empathic resilience. All figures and causal-language nuance correctly carried over.

entries.title: Intellectual Humility and Responsiveness to Public Health Recommendations
entries.design: two correlational survey studies during COVID-19 pandemic
entries.evidence_level: correlational, cross-sectional, general population, non-relationship context
entries.population_setting: US adult samples, Study 1 N=541, Study 2 N ranging 265-702
entries.finding: Higher intellectual humility associated with greater adherence to expert health recommendations (mask-wearing, social distancing) even controlling for political affiliation; association partly mediated by beliefs that mask-wearing is effective and protects others; IH also associated with prosocial traits (agreeableness, benevolence).
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports R1 humility as a construct linked to health-behaviour uptake and openness to correction from external/expert sources, an analogy to T-PHE's claim that humility supports responsiveness to health education content; note this is about deference to public-health expertise, not to a partner or facilitator in an intimate/premarital context, so the analogy is domain-shifted.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: Study 1 N=541 matches; 'people higher in IH are more likely to engage in recommended health behaviors... even when controlling for political affiliation'; mediation by beliefs mask-wearing is effective/protects others; Study 2 (Ns 265-702) IH linked to agreeableness/benevolence. Relevance correctly flags this is deference to public-health expertise, not to a partner/facilitator -- domain-shifted analogy.

entries.title: A Theory of Cultural Humility
entries.design: theory-development paper using Walker and Avant concept/theory-synthesis method
entries.evidence_level: theoretical/conceptual synthesis, no empirical outcome data
entries.population_setting: nursing and health-professions education, theoretical/conceptual (no primary human sample)
entries.finding: Presents a synthesized theory of cultural humility (antecedents, attributes, outcomes) intended to guide nurses and other professions toward improved cross-cultural interactions and reduced conflict from misunderstood differences in perspective.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports R1/R4: extends cultural humility beyond the foundational Tervalon 1998 formulation with a structured theory of humility's mechanism and outcomes in health-professional practice, relevant to T-PHE's facilitator-side humility/restraint safeguard; it is theoretical, not an outcomes study, so it complicates any claim of measured effect.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms theory-development paper (Walker & Avant method), no primary human sample, presents 'a theory to guide nurses and other professions on how to appreciate diversity and apply cultural humility.' Correctly flagged as theoretical/no empirical outcome data.

entries.title: Rethinking Cultural Competence: Shifting to Cultural Humility
entries.design: narrative literature review/position paper
entries.evidence_level: narrative review/position paper, not a controlled outcomes study
entries.population_setting: healthcare and social-services providers, conceptual review
entries.finding: Review argues cultural competence training has limited demonstrated effectiveness and risks stereotyping/othering patients; proposes cultural humility (self-reflexivity, sharing power with patients, continuous learning) as an alternative orientation to care, going beyond the original Tervalon 1998 formulation into critique of competence-based training outcomes.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports R4 restraint/mechanism decision control: cultural humility framed explicitly as power-sharing and continuous self-correction, an analogy for T-PHE's facilitator conscientious self-restraint (conscientious self-restraint) in using programme authority/knowledge; complicates T-PHE by showing competence-training evidence base itself is weak, cautioning against assuming humility framing alone guarantees outcomes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'a review of the literature highlights the limited effectiveness of cultural competence training'; proposes cultural humility as 'self-reflexivity... openness to sharing power with patients, and to continue learning.' Matches key_finding; correctly labeled narrative review/position paper.

entries.title: S.E.L.F.: Lessons in institutional cultural humility approach from an academic health center
entries.design: programme evaluation of an institutional cultural-humility training module (mixed quantitative/qualitative)
entries.evidence_level: pre/post programme evaluation, self-reported attitudes/knowledge/satisfaction, no control group reported in abstract
entries.population_setting: 30,000 employees across a large US health system
entries.finding: Institution-wide cultural humility training module showed improved attitudes, knowledge and satisfaction post-training; qualitative analysis highlighted perceived utility; authors emphasize a single training is insufficient and ongoing education/dialogue is needed for institutional culture change and accountability.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports R1 humility with an actual outcomes-evaluation beyond Tervalon 1998's conceptual paper, at institutional/health-system scale; also cautions (complicates) T-PHE's implicit assumption that a bounded programme intervention alone can institutionalize humility, since this study explicitly found single-dose training insufficient.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: '30,000 employees across a health system'; 'positive outcomes, including improved attitudes, knowledge, and satisfaction'; 'Contrary to the belief that a single training is sufficient, this evaluation underscores the importance of continuous learning and dialogue.' Matches key_finding and the complicating caution exactly.

entries.title: Exploring compassion: a meta-analysis of the association between self-compassion and psychopathology
entries.design: systematic review and meta-analysis (random-effects), 20 samples from 14 studies, all using the Neff Self-Compassion Scale
entries.evidence_level: meta-analysis of correlational studies (Th2-equivalent quantitative synthesis, not causal/RCT evidence)
entries.population_setting: mixed clinical/non-clinical adult samples across included studies
entries.finding: Large inverse effect size between self-compassion and psychopathology, r=-0.54 (95% CI -0.57 to -0.51, p<.0001); no evidence of significant publication bias; significant heterogeneity across studies.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the compassion node of T-PHE's sequence (acknowledging one's own limits -> humility/compassion) with strong quantitative meta-analytic evidence for compassion's mental-health benefit; this is evidence for self-compassion and mental health generally, not for T-PHE's premarital programme itself — an analogy, not direct support.
entries.verifier_note: STRICT EFFECT-SIZE CHECK CONFIRMED. Abstract: 'a large effect size for the relationship between compassion and psychopathology of r=-0.54 (95% CI=-0.57 to -0.51; Z=-34.02; p<.0001)... no evidence of significant publication bias.' 20 samples/14 studies matches. Correctly labeled meta-analysis of correlational studies, not causal/RCT evidence.

entries.title: The effectiveness of compassion focused therapy with clinical populations: A systematic review and meta-analysis
entries.design: systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of RCTs and randomised pilot/feasibility studies, 15 studies (2013-2022)
entries.evidence_level: meta-analysis of RCTs/pilot RCTs (Th1-equivalent for the CFT-outcome link), moderate quality concerns noted by authors
entries.population_setting: clinical populations with mental health difficulties, mixed settings; ~75% female participants
entries.finding: Compassion Focused Therapy (CFT) improved self-compassion (effect sizes 0.19-0.90), self-criticism (0.15-0.72), self-reassurance (0.43-0.81), and reduced clinical symptomology (e.g. depression 0.24-0.25) versus waitlist control; 7/15 studies rated unclear methodological quality; long-term effects not established.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports compassion as a modifiable, intervention-responsive construct with measured clinical benefit (RCT-level evidence), the strongest causal analogue among the compassion records for T-PHE's claim that compassion-building content could plausibly improve wellbeing; complicates by flagging unclear-quality studies and absence of long-term follow-up, cautioning against overclaiming durability.
entries.verifier_note: STRICT DESIGN CHECK CONFIRMED. Abstract explicitly says the review covers 'randomised controlled trials and randomised pilot/feasibility studies' (15 studies, 2013-2022) -- key_finding correctly avoids calling this a pure-RCT meta-analysis. Effect sizes self-compassion 0.19-0.90, self-criticism 0.15-0.72, self-reassurance 0.43-0.81, depression 0.24-0.25 all match verbatim. Abstract says '74.88%... female participants'; record rounds to '~75% female', acceptable rounding. '7/15... unclear' quality and no long-term-effects claim both match.

entries.title: Self-compassion and relationship maintenance: the moderating roles of conscientiousness and gender
entries.journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
entries.design: two correlational studies, one experiment, one longitudinal study
entries.evidence_level: mixed correlational, experimental and longitudinal design (multi-study), general (non-premarital, non-Muslim, non-Thai) samples
entries.population_setting: romantic couples/intimates, mixed community samples (US)
entries.finding: Among men high in conscientiousness, self-compassion was associated with greater motivation to correct interpersonal mistakes, more constructive problem-solving, more accommodation, and fewer declines in marital satisfaction; among men low in conscientiousness, associations reversed; among women, self-compassion was positively associated with corrective motivation and satisfaction change regardless of conscientiousness.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates a simple 'more compassion is always better' reading of T-PHE's safeguard: shows self-compassion's relational benefit is conditional on conscientiousness (a self-regulation trait), suggesting T-PHE's safeguard sequence (compassion feeding into restraint) may need conscientiousness/self-regulation as a moderating condition, not an automatic consequence, especially for men in this sample.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms conscientiousness-moderation pattern for men (high conscientiousness -> self-compassion helps; low -> reverses) and unconditional positive association for women. Multi-study design (2 correlational + 1 experiment + 1 longitudinal) matches. Relevance correctly uses this to complicate a naive 'more compassion is always better' reading of T-PHE's safeguard.

entries.title: Relationship satisfaction in Black heterosexual couples: The role of self-compassion and openness
entries.journal: Journal of marital and family therapy
entries.design: cross-sectional dyadic survey, common-fate moderated mediation model
entries.evidence_level: cross-sectional dyadic survey with moderated-mediation modeling, married (not premarital) US Black couples
entries.population_setting: 210 Black married heterosexual couples, US
entries.finding: Higher self-compassion in both spouses associated with lower negative interaction in the relationship; couples' negative interaction suppressed the positive effect of self-compassion on relationship satisfaction; for wives, open communication moderated how self-compassion related to satisfaction, and this pathway depended on perceived racial discrimination.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates a straightforward compassion-to-satisfaction claim: shows the compassion -> satisfaction pathway can be suppressed by negative interaction and is contingent on open communication and external stressors (discrimination) — evidence that T-PHE's safeguard sequence likely needs supporting conditions (open communication, low conflict) to translate compassion into relational benefit, not a direct or guaranteed chain.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms: 210 Black married heterosexual couples; higher self-compassion in both spouses -> lower negative interaction; negative interaction suppressed the positive effect on satisfaction; for wives, open communication and perceived discrimination moderate the pathway. entries.title: Empathy Mediates the Relations between Working Memory and Perpetration of Intimate Partner Violence and Aggression
entries.design: laboratory-based observational study with conflict-discussion coding and self/partner-report
entries.evidence_level: observational/mediation analysis, small sample, single study (not meta-analytic)
entries.population_setting: 49 men in heterosexual relationships, community sample
entries.finding: Working memory positively related to cognitive and affective empathy and negatively related to men's physical abuse perpetration and observed aggression; effects of working memory on aggression and IPV frequency were fully mediated by empathy (cognitive/affective respectively).
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the theoretical rationale for R4/mechanism decision control: empathy (a compassion-adjacent construct) mediating the link between cognitive-executive deficits and IPV perpetration supports the plausibility that fostering empathy/compassion could reduce coercive or aggressive relational behaviour, an analogy for why T-PHE positions compassion as protective; small sample (N=49), so effect sizes should not be generalized.
entries.verifier_note: EMPATHY-IPV DIRECTION CHECK CONFIRMED. Abstract: N=49 men; 'working memory was positively related to cognitive and affective empathy, and negatively related to men's physical abuse perpetration and observed aggression'; effects of working memory on aggression/IPV 'fully mediated by' empathy. Direction of empathy-IPV association (protective) matches; small-N caveat correctly flagged.

entries.title: Childhood Sexual Abuse, Dyadic Empathy, and Intimate Partner Violence Among Men Seeking Psychological Help
entries.design: cross-sectional survey with mediation/moderation analysis
entries.evidence_level: cross-sectional, clinical help-seeking sample, single study
entries.population_setting: 198 men aged 18-69 seeking help for relationship problems (clinical/help-seeking sample)
entries.finding: Emotional empathy mediated and moderated the link between childhood sexual abuse (CSA) and perpetrated psychological (not physical) IPV; cognitive empathy negatively associated with both physical and psychological IPV, while emotional empathy was positively associated with psychological IPV, showing a complex, construct-specific pattern.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates a simple 'empathy reduces IPV' narrative that would support T-PHE's compassion safeguard: shows emotional empathy can be positively associated with psychological IPV perpetration in a help-seeking clinical sample, while cognitive empathy is protective — evidence that compassion/empathy constructs are not uniformly protective and must be specified (cognitive vs emotional) when used to ground a safeguard.
entries.verifier_note: EMPATHY-IPV DIRECTION CHECK CONFIRMED, construct-specific. Abstract: N=198 men; 'cognitive empathy was negatively associated with physical and psychological IPV, whereas emotional empathy was positively associated with psychological IPV'; emotional empathy mediated/moderated CSA->psychological IPV, cognitive empathy only moderated. The record's key_finding and relevance correctly reject a simple 'empathy always protects' narrative and specify cognitive vs emotional empathy -- this is exactly the nuance the abstract supports.

entries.title: ADHD in Childhood and/or Adulthood as a Risk Factor for Domestic Violence or Intimate Partner Violence: A Systematic Review
entries.design: systematic review of case-control and cohort studies
entries.evidence_level: systematic review of case-control/cohort studies (Th2-equivalent, observational only, not RCT)
